entries.9776ee2ea537a74332d7eb6535047a614d99b3ac: <div sID="gen9599" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="15" osisID="Job.15" sID="Job.15"/> <div eID="gen9599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9600" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9601" type="x-p"/> Perhaps Job was so clear, and so well satisfied, in the goodness of his own cause, that he thought, if he had not convinced, yet he had at least silenced all his three friends; but, it seems he had not: in this chapter they begin a second attack upon him, each of them charging him afresh with as much vehemence as before. It is natural to us to be fond of our own sentiments, and therefore to be firm to them, and with difficulty to be brought to recede from them. Eliphaz here keeps close to the principles upon which he had condemned Job, and, I. He reproves him for justifying himself, and fathers on him many evil things which are unfairly inferred thence, <reference osisRef="Job.15.2-Job.15.13">ver. 2-13</reference>. II. He persuades him to humble himself before God and to take shame to himself, <reference osisRef="Job.15.14-Job.15.16">ver. 14-16</reference>. III. He reads him a long lecture concerning the woeful estate of wicked people, who harden their hearts against God and the judgments which are prepared for them, <reference osisRef="Job.15.17-Job.15.25">ver. 17-35</reference>. A good use may be made both of his reproofs (for they are plain) and of his doctrine (for it is sound), though both the one and the other are misapplied to Job.
entries.12044b27aad8faab6ff89ae5d0aebd954d0fbe38: <div eID="gen9601" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9600" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Second Address of Eliphaz. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9602" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then answered Eliphaz the Temanite, and said, 2 Should a wise man utter vain knowledge, and fill his belly with the east wind? <hi type="super">3</hi> Should he reason with unprofitable talk? or with speeches wherewith he can do no good? <hi type="super">4</hi> Yea, thou castest off fear, and restrainest prayer before God. <hi type="super">5</hi> For thy mouth uttereth thine iniquity, and thou choosest the tongue of the crafty. <hi type="super">6</hi> Thine own mouth condemneth thee, and not I: yea, thine own lips testify against thee. <hi type="super">7</hi> <hi type="italic">Art</hi> thou the first man <hi type="italic">that</hi> was born? or wast thou made before the hills? <hi type="super">8</hi> Hast thou heard the secret of God? and dost thou restrain wisdom to thyself? <hi type="super">9</hi> What knowest thou, that we know not? <hi type="italic">what</hi> understandest thou, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> not in us? <hi type="super">10</hi> With us <hi type="italic">are</hi> both the grayheaded and very aged men, much elder than thy father. <hi type="super">11</hi> <hi type="italic">Are</hi> the consolations of God small with thee? is there any secret thing with thee? <hi type="super">12</hi> Why doth thine heart carry thee away? and what do thy eyes wink at, <hi type="super">13</hi> That thou turnest thy spirit against God, and lettest <hi type="italic">such</hi> words go out of thy mouth? <hi type="super">14</hi> What <hi type="italic">is</hi> man, that he should be clean? and <hi type="italic">he which is</hi> born of a woman, that he should be righteous? <hi type="super">15</hi> Behold, he putteth no trust in his saints; yea, the heavens are not clean in his sight. <hi type="super">16</hi> How much more abominable and filthy <hi type="italic">is</hi> man, which drinketh iniquity like water? <div eID="gen9602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9603" type="x-p"/> Eliphaz here falls very foul upon Job, because he contradicted what he and his colleagues had said, and did not acquiesce in it and applaud it, as they expected. Proud people are apt thus to take it very much amiss if they may not have leave to dictate and give law to all about them, and to censure those as ignorant and obstinate, and all that is naught, who cannot in every thing say as they say. Several great crimes Eliphaz here charges Job with, only because he would not own himself a hypocrite. <div eID="gen9603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9604" type="x-p"/> I. He charges him with folly and absurdity (<reference osisRef="Job.15.2-Job.15.3">v. 2, 3</reference>), that, whereas he had been reputed a wise man, he had now quite forfeited his reputation; any one would say that his wisdom had departed from him, he talked so extravagantly and so little to the purpose. Bildad began thus (<reference osisRef="Job.8.2">ch. viii. 2</reference>), and Zophar, <reference osisRef="Job.11.2-Job.11.3">ch. xi. 2, 3</reference>. It is common for angry disputants thus to represent one another's reasonings as impertinent and ridiculous more than there is cause, forgetting the doom of him that calls his brother <hi type="italic">Raca,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Thou fool.</hi> It is true, 1. That there is in the world a great deal of vain knowledge, science falsely so called, that is useless, and therefore worthless. 2. That this is the knowledge that puffs up, with which men swell in a fond conceit of their own accomplishments. 3. That, whatever vain knowledge a man may have in his head, if he would be thought a wise man he must not utter it, but let it die with himself as it deserves. 4. Unprofitable talk is evil talk. We must give an account in the great day not only for wicked words, but for idle words. Speeches therefore which do no good, which do no service either to God or our neighbour, or no justice to ourselves, which are no way to the use of edifying, were better unspoken. Those words which are as wind, light and empty, especially which are as the east wind, hurtful and pernicious, it will be pernicious to fill either ourselves or others with, for they will pass very ill in the account. 5. Vain knowledge or unprofitable talk ought to be reproved and checked, especially in a wise man, whom it worst becomes and who does most hurt by the bad example of it. <div eID="gen9604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9605" type="x-p"/> II. He charges him with impiety and irreligion (<reference osisRef="Job.15.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou castest off fear,</hi>" that is, "the fear of God, and that regard to him which thou shouldst have; and then <hi type="italic">thou restrainest prayer.</hi>" See what religion is summed up in, fearing God and praying to him, the former the most needful principle, the latter the most needful practice. Where no fear of God is no good is to be expected; and those who live without prayer certainly live without God in the world. Those who restrain prayer do thereby give evidence that they cast off fear. Surely those have no reverence of God's majesty, no dread of his wrath, and are in no care about their souls and eternity, who make no applications to God for his grace. Those who are prayerless are fearless and graceless. When the fear of God is cast off all sin is let in and a door opened to all manner of profaneness. It is especially bad with those who have had some fear of God, but have now cast it off—have been frequent in prayer, but now restrain it. How have they fallen! How is their first love lost! It denotes a kind of force put upon themselves. The fear of God would cleave to them, but they throw it off; prayer would be uttered, but they restrain it; and, in both, they baffle their convictions. Those who either omit prayer or straiten and abridge themselves in it, quenching the spirit of adoption and denying themselves the liberty they might take in the duty, restrain prayer. This is bad enough, but it is worse to restrain others from prayer, to prohibit and discourage prayer, as Darius, <reference osisRef="Dan.6.7">Dan. vi. 7</reference>. Now, <div eID="gen9605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9606" type="x-p"/> 1. Eliphaz charges this upon Job, either, (1.) As that which was his own practice. He thought that Job talked of God with such liberty as if he had been his equal, and that he charged him so vehemently with hard usage of him, and challenged him so often to a fair trial, that he had quite thrown off all religious regard to him. This charge was utterly false, and yet wanted not some colour. We ought not only to take care that we keep up prayer and the fear of God, but that we never drop any unwary expressions which may give occasion to those who seek occasion to question our sincerity and constancy in religion. Or, (2.) As that which others would infer from the doctrine he maintained. "If this be true" (thinks Eliphaz) "which Job says, that a man may be thus sorely afflicted and yet be a good man, then farewell all religion, farewell prayer and the fear of God. If all things come alike to all, and the best men may have the worst treatment in this world, every one will be ready to say, <hi type="italic">It is vain to serve God; and what profit is it to keep his ordinances?</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.3.14">Mal. iii. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">Verily I have cleansed my hands in vain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.73.13-Ps.73.14">Ps. lxxiii. 13, 14</reference>. Who will be honest if the tabernacles of robbers prosper? <reference osisRef="Job.12.6">ch. xii. 6</reference>. If there be no forgiveness with God (<reference osisRef="Job.7.21">ch. vii. 21</reference>), who will fear him? <reference osisRef="Ps.130.4">Ps. cxxx. 4</reference>. If he <hi type="italic">laugh at the trial of the innocent</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.9.23">ch. ix. 23</reference>), if he be so difficult of access (<reference osisRef="Job.9.32">ch. ix. 32</reference>), who will pray to him?" Note, It is a piece of injustice which even wise and good men are too often guilty of, in the heat of disputation, to charge upon their adversaries those consequences of their opinions which are not fairly drawn from them and which really they abhor. This is not doing as we would be done by. <div eID="gen9606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9607" type="x-p"/> 2. Upon this strained innuendo Eliphaz grounds that high charge of impiety (<reference osisRef="Job.15.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thy mouth utters thy iniquity—teaches it,</hi> so the word is. "Thou teachest others to have the same hard thoughts of God and religion that thou thyself hast." It is bad to <hi type="italic">break even the least of the commandments,</hi> but worse to <hi type="italic">teach men so,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.5.19">Matt. v. 19</reference>. If we ever thought evil, let us lay our hand upon our mouth to suppress the evil thought (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.32">Prov. xxx. 32</reference>), and let us by no means utter it; that is putting an <hi type="italic">imprimatur</hi> to it, publishing it with allowance, to the dishonour of God and the damage of others. Observe, When men have cast off fear and prayer their mouths utter iniquity. Those that cease to do good soon learn to do evil. What can we expect but all manner of iniquity from those that arm not themselves with the grace of God against it? But <hi type="italic">thou choosest the tongue of the crafty,</hi> that is, "Thou utterest thy iniquity with some show and pretence of piety, mixing some good words with the bad, as tradesmen do with their wares to help them off." The mouth of iniquity could not do so much mischief as it does without the tongue of the crafty. The serpent beguiled Eve through his subtlety. See <reference osisRef="Rom.16.18">Rom. xvi. 18</reference>. The tongue of the crafty speaks with design and deliberation; and therefore those that use it may be said to <hi type="italic">choose</hi> it, as that which will serve their purpose better than the tongue of the upright: but it will be found, at last, that honesty is the best policy. Eliphaz, in his first discourse, had proceeded against Job upon mere surmise (<reference osisRef="Job.4.6-Job.4.7">ch. iv. 6, 7</reference>), but now he has got proof against him from his own discourses (<reference osisRef="Job.15.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thy own mouth condemns thee, and not I.</hi> But he should have considered that he and his fellows had provoked him to say that which now they took advantage of; and that was not fair. Those are most effectually condemned that are condemned by themselves, <reference osisRef="Titus.3.11">Tit. iii. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.19.22">Luke xix. 22</reference>. Many a man needs no more to sink him than for his own tongue to fall upon him. <div eID="gen9607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9608" type="x-p"/> III. He charges him with intolerable arrogancy and self-conceitedness. It was a just, and reasonable, and modest demand that Job had made (<reference osisRef="Job.12.3">ch. xii. 3</reference>), Allow that <hi type="italic">I have understanding as well as you;</hi> but see how they seek occasion against him: that is misconstrued, as if he pretended to be wiser than any man. Because he will not grant to them the monopoly of wisdom, they will have it thought that he claims it to himself, <reference osisRef="Job.15.7-Job.15.9">v. 7-9</reference>. As if he thought he had the advantage of all mankind, 1. In length of acquaintance with the world, which furnishes men with so much the more experience: "<hi type="italic">Art thou the first man that was born;</hi> and, consequently, senior to us, and better able to give the sense of antiquity and the judgment of the first and earliest, the wisest and purest, ages? Art thou prior to Adam?" So it may be read. "Did not he suffer for sin; and yet wilt not thou, who art so great a sufferer, own thyself a sinner? <hi type="italic">Wast thou made before the hills,</hi> as Wisdom herself was? <reference osisRef="Prov.8.23">Prov. viii. 23</reference>, &c. Must God's counsels, which are as the great mountains (<reference osisRef="Ps.36.6">Ps. xxxvi. 6</reference>), and immovable as the everlasting hills, be subject to thy notions and bow to them? Dost thou know more of the world than any of us do? No, thou art but of yesterday even as we are," <reference osisRef="Job.8.9">ch. viii. 9</reference>. Or, 2. In intimacy of acquaintance with God (<reference osisRef="Job.15.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Hast thou heard the secret of God?</hi> Dost thou pretend to be of the cabinet-council of heaven, that thou canst give better reasons than others can for God's proceedings?" There are secret things of God, which belong not to us, and which therefore we must not pretend to account for. Those are daringly presumptuous who do. He also represents him, (1.) As assuming to himself such knowledge as none else had: "<hi type="italic">Dost thou restrain wisdom to thyself,</hi> as if none were wise besides?" Job had said (<reference osisRef="Job.13.2">ch. xiii. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">What you know, the same do I know also;</hi> and now they return upon him, according to the usage of eager disputants, who think they have a privilege to commend themselves: <hi type="italic">What knowest thou that we know not?</hi> How natural are such replies as these in the heat of argument! But how simple do they look afterwards, upon the review! (2.) As opposing the stream of antiquity, a venerable name, under the shade of which all contending parties strive to shelter themselves: "<hi type="italic">With us are the gray-headed and very aged men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.15.10">v. 10</reference>. We have the fathers on our side; all the ancient doctors of the church are of our opinion." A thing soon said, but not so soon proved; and, when proved, truth is not so soon discovered and proved by it as most people imagine. David preferred right scripture-knowledge before that of antiquity (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.100">Ps. cxix. 100</reference>): <hi type="italic">I understand more than the ancients, because I keep thy precepts.</hi> Or perhaps one or more, if not all three, of these friends of Job, were older than he (<reference osisRef="Job.32.6">ch. xxxii. 6</reference>), and therefore they thought he was bound to acknowledge them to be in the right. This also serves contenders to make a noise with to very little purpose. If they are older than their adversaries, and can say they knew such a thing before their opponents were born, this will not serve to justify them in being arrogant and overbearing; for the oldest are not always the wisest, <reference osisRef="Job.32.9">ch. xxxii. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen9608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9609" type="x-p"/> IV. He charges him with a contempt of the counsels and comforts that were given him by his friends (<reference osisRef="Job.15.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Are the consolations of God small with thee?</hi> 1. Eliphaz takes it ill that Job did not value the comforts which he and his friends administered to him more than it seems he did, and did not welcome every word they said as true and important. It is true they had said some very good things, but, in their application to Job, they were miserable comforters. Note, We are apt to think that great and considerable which we ourselves say, when others perhaps with good reason think it small and trifling. Paul found that those who <hi type="italic">seemed to be somewhat, yet, in conference, added nothing to him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.2.6">Gal. ii. 6</reference>. 2. He represents this as a slight put upon divine consolations in general, as if they were of small account with him, whereas really they were not. If he had not highly valued them, he could not have borne up as he did under his sufferings. Note, (1.) The consolations of God are not in themselves small. Divine comforts are great things, that is, the comfort which is from God, especially the comfort which is in God. (2.) The consolations of God not being small in themselves, it is very lamentable if they be small with us. It is a great affront to God, and an evidence of a degenerate depraved mind, to disesteem and undervalue spiritual delights and despise the pleasant land. "What!" (says Eliphaz) "<hi type="italic">is there any secret thing with thee?</hi> Hast thou some cordial to support thyself with, that is a <hi type="italic">proprium,</hi> an <hi type="italic">arcanum,</hi> that nobody else can pretend to, or knows any thing of?" Or, "Is there some secret sin harboured and indulged in thy bosom, which hinders the operation of divine comforts?" None disesteem divine comforts but those that secretly affect the world and the flesh. <div eID="gen9609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9610" type="x-p"/> V. He charges him with opposition to God himself and to religion (<reference osisRef="Job.15.12-Job.15.13">v. 12, 13</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Why doth thy heart carry thee away</hi> into such indecent irreligious expressions?" Note, <hi type="italic">Every man is tempted when he is drawn away of his own lust,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.1.14">Jam. i. 14</reference>. If we fly off from God and our duty, or fly out into anything amiss, it is our own heart that carries us away. <hi type="italic">If thou scornest, thou alone shalt bear it.</hi> There is a violence, an ungovernable impetus, in the turnings of the soul; the corrupt heart carries men away, as it were, by force, against their convictions. "What is it that thy eyes wink at? Why so careless and mindless of what is said to thee, hearing it as if thou wert half asleep? Why so scornful, disdaining what we say, as if it were below thee to take notice of it? What have we said that deserves to be thus slighted—nay, <hi type="italic">that thou turnest thy spirit against God?</hi>" It was bad that his heart was carried away from God, but much worse that it was turned against God. But those that forsake God will soon break out in open enmity to him. But how did this appear? Why, "Thou lettest such words go out of thy mouth, reflecting on God, and his justice and goodness." It is the character of the wicked that they <hi type="italic">set their mouth against the heavens</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.9">Ps. lxxiii. 9</reference>), which is a certain indication that the spirit is turned against God. He thought Job's spirit was soured against God, and so turned from what it had been, and exasperated at his dealings with him. Eliphaz wanted candour and charity, else he would not have put such a harsh construction upon the speeches of one that had such a settled reputation for piety and was now in temptation. This was, in effect, to give the cause on Satan's side, and to own that Job had done as Satan said he would, had <hi type="italic">cursed God to his face.</hi> <div eID="gen9610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9611" type="x-p"/> VI. He charges him with justifying himself to such a degree as even to deny his share in the common corruption and pollution of the human nature (<reference osisRef="Job.15.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">What is man, that he should be clean?</hi> that is, that he should pretend to be so, or that any should expect to find him so. What is <hi type="italic">he that is born of a woman,</hi> a sinful woman, <hi type="italic">that he should be righteous?</hi> Note, 1. Righteousness is cleanness; it makes us acceptable to God and easy to ourselves, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.24">Ps. xviii. 24</reference>. 2. Man, in his fallen state, cannot pretend to be clean and righteous before God, either to acquit himself to God's justice or recommend himself to his favour. 3. He is to be adjudged unclean and unrighteous because born of a woman, from whom he derives a corrupt nature, which is both his guilt and his pollution. With these plain truths Eliphaz thinks to convince Job, whereas he had just now said the same (<reference osisRef="Job.14.4">ch. xiv. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?</hi> But does it therefore follow that Job is a hypocrite, and a wicked man, which is all that he denied? By no means. Though man, as born of a woman, is not clean, yet, as born again of the Spirit, he is clean. 4. Further to evince this he here shows, (1.) That the brightest creatures are imperfect and impure before God, <reference osisRef="Job.15.15">v. 15</reference>. God places no confidence in saints and angels; he employs both, but trusts neither with his service, without giving them fresh supplies of strength and wisdom for it, as knowing they are not sufficient of themselves, neither more nor better than his grace makes them. He takes no complacency in the heavens themselves. How pure soever they seem to us, in his eye they have many a speck and many a flaw: <hi type="italic">The heavens are not clean in his sight.</hi> If the stars (says Mr. Caryl) have no light in the sight of the sun, what light has the sun in the sight of God! See <reference osisRef="Isa.24.23">Isa. xxiv. 23</reference>. (2.) That man is much more so (<reference osisRef="Job.15.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">How much more abominable and filthy is man!</hi> If saints are not to be trusted, much less sinners. If the heavens are not pure, which are as God made them, much less man, who is degenerated. Nay, he is abominable and filthy in the sight of God, and if ever he repent he is so in his own sight, and therefore he abhors himself. Sin is an odious thing, it makes men hateful. The body of sin is so, and is therefore called <hi type="italic">a dead body,</hi> a loathsome thing. Is it not a filthy thing, and enough to make any one sick, to see a man eating swine's food or drinking some nauseous and offensive stuff? Such is the filthiness of man that he <hi type="italic">drinks iniquity</hi> (that abominable thing which the Lord hates) as greedily, and with as much pleasure, as a man drinks water when he is thirsty. It is his constant drink; it is natural to sinners to commit iniquity. It gratifies, but does not satisfy, the appetites of the old man. It is like water to a man in a dropsy. The more men sin the more they would sin.
entries.a1fa101bd93105cedc5bed37a55cd95b5e8d0d19: <div eID="gen9611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9612" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> I will show thee, hear me; and that <hi type="italic">which</hi> I have seen I will declare; <hi type="super">18</hi> Which wise men have told from their fathers, and have not hid <hi type="italic">it:</hi> <hi type="super">19</hi> Unto whom alone the earth was given, and no stranger passed among them. <hi type="super">20</hi> The wicked man travaileth with pain all <hi type="italic">his</hi> days, and the number of years is hidden to the oppressor. <hi type="super">21</hi> A dreadful sound <hi type="italic">is</hi> in his ears: in prosperity the destroyer shall come upon him. <hi type="super">22</hi> He believeth not that he shall return out of darkness, and he is waited for of the sword. <hi type="super">23</hi> He wandereth abroad for bread, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> Where <hi type="italic">is it?</hi> he knoweth that the day of darkness is ready at his hand. 24 Trouble and anguish shall make him afraid; they shall prevail against him, as a king ready to the battle. <hi type="super">25</hi> For he stretcheth out his hand against God, and strengtheneth himself against the Almighty. <hi type="super">26</hi> He runneth upon him, <hi type="italic">even</hi> on <hi type="italic">his</hi> neck, upon the thick bosses of his bucklers: <hi type="super">27</hi> Because he covereth his face with his fatness, and maketh collops of fat on <hi type="italic">his</hi> flanks. <hi type="super">28</hi> And he dwelleth in desolate cities, <hi type="italic">and</hi> in houses which no man inhabiteth, which are ready to become heaps. <hi type="super">29</hi> He shall not be rich, neither shall his substance continue, neither shall he prolong the perfection thereof upon the earth. <hi type="super">30</hi> He shall not depart out of darkness; the flame shall dry up his branches, and by the breath of his mouth shall he go away. <hi type="super">31</hi> Let not him that is deceived trust in vanity: for vanity shall be his recompence. 32 It shall be accomplished before his time, and his branch shall not be green. <hi type="super">33</hi> He shall shake off his unripe grape as the vine, and shall cast off his flower as the olive. <hi type="super">34</hi> For the congregation of hypocrites <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> desolate, and fire shall consume the tabernacles of bribery. <hi type="super">35</hi> They conceive mischief, and bring forth vanity, and their belly prepareth deceit. <div eID="gen9612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9613" type="x-p"/> Eliphaz, having reproved Job for his answers, here comes to maintain his own thesis, upon which he built his censure of Job. His opinion is that those who are wicked are certainly miserable, whence he would infer that those who are miserable are certainly wicked, and that therefore Job was so. Observe, <div eID="gen9613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9614" type="x-p"/> I. His solemn preface to this discourse, in which he bespeaks Job's attention, which he had little reason to expect, he having given so little heed to and put so little value upon what Job had said (<reference osisRef="Job.15.17">v. 17</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will show thee</hi> that which is worth hearing, and not reason, as thou dost, with unprofitable talk." Thus apt are men, when they condemn the reasonings of others, to commend their own. He promises to teach him, 1. From his own experience and observation: "<hi type="italic">That which I have</hi> myself <hi type="italic">seen,</hi> in divers instances, <hi type="italic">I will declare.</hi>" It is of good use to take notice of the providences of God concerning the children of men, from which many a good lesson may be learned. What good observations we have made, and have found benefit by ourselves, we should be ready to communicate for the benefit of others; and we may speak boldly when we declare what we have seen. 2. From the wisdom of the ancients (<reference osisRef="Job.15.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">Which wise men have told from their fathers.</hi> Note, The wisdom and learning of the moderns are very much derived from those of the ancients. Good children will learn a good deal from their good parents; and what we have learned from our ancestors we must transmit to our posterity and not hide from the generations to come. See <reference osisRef="Ps.78.3-Ps.78.6">Ps. lxxviii. 3-6</reference>. If the thread of the knowledge of many ages be cut off by the carelessness of one, and nothing be done to preserve it pure and entire, all that succeed fare the worse. The authorities Eliphaz vouched were authorities indeed, men of rank and figure (<reference osisRef="Job.15.19">v. 19</reference>), <hi type="italic">unto whom alone the earth was given,</hi> and therefore you may suppose them favourites of Heaven and best capable of making observations concerning the affairs of this earth. The dictates of wisdom come with advantage from those who are in places of dignity and power, as Solomon; yet there is a wisdom <hi type="italic">which none of the princes of this world knew,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.7-1Cor.2.8">1 Cor. ii. 7, 8</reference>. <div eID="gen9614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9615" type="x-p"/> II. The discourse itself. He here aims to show, <div eID="gen9615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9616" type="x-p"/> 1. That those who are wise and good do ordinarily prosper in this world. This he only hints at (<reference osisRef="Job.15.19">v. 19</reference>), that those of whose mind he was were such as had the earth given to them, and to them only; they enjoyed it entirely and peaceably, and no stranger passed among them, either to share with them or give disturbance to them. Job had said, <hi type="italic">The earth is given into the hand of the wicked,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.9.24">ch. ix. 24</reference>. "No," says Eliphaz, "it is given into the hands of the saints, and runs along with the faith committed unto them; and they are not robbed and plundered by strangers and enemies making inroads upon them, as thou art by the Sabeans and Chaldeans." But because many of God's people have remarkably prospered in this world, as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, it does not therefore follow that those who are crossed and impoverished, as Job, are not God's people. <div eID="gen9616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9617" type="x-p"/> 2. That wicked people, and particularly oppressors and tyrannizing rulers, are subject to continual terrors, live very uncomfortably, and perish very miserably. On this head he enlarges, showing that even those who impiously dare God's judgments yet cannot but dread them and will feel them at last. He speaks in the singular number—<hi type="italic">the wicked man,</hi> meaning (as some think) Nimrod; or perhaps Chedorlaomer, or some such mighty hunter before the Lord. I fear he meant Job himself, whom he expressly charges both with the tyranny and with the timorousness here described, <reference osisRef="Job.22.9-Job.22.10">ch. xxii. 9, 10</reference>. Here he thinks the application easy, and that Job might, in this description, as in a glass, see his own face. Now, <div eID="gen9617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9618" type="x-p"/> (1.) Let us see how he describes the sinner who lives thus miserably. He does not begin with that, but brings it in as a reason of his doom, <reference osisRef="Job.15.25-Job.15.28">v. 25-28</reference>. It is no ordinary sinner, but one of the first rate, an <hi type="italic">oppressor</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.15.20">v. 20</reference>), a <hi type="italic">blasphemer, and a persecutor,</hi> one that <hi type="italic">neither fears God nor regards man.</hi> [1.] He bids defiance to God, and to his authority and power, <reference osisRef="Job.15.25">v. 25</reference>. Tell him of the divine law, and its obligations; he breaks those bonds asunder, and will not have, no, not him that made him, to restrain him or rule over him. Tell him of the divine wrath, and its terrors; he bids the Almighty do his worst, he will have his will, he will have his way, in spite of him, and will not be controlled by law, or conscience, or the notices of a judgment to come. <hi type="italic">He stretches out his hand against God,</hi> in defiance of him and of the power of his wrath. God is indeed out of his reach, but he stretches out his hand against him, to show that, if it were in his power, he would ungod him. This applies to the audacious impiety of some sinners who are really <hi type="italic">haters of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.30">Rom. i. 30</reference>), and whose carnal mind is not only an enemy to him, but enmity itself, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.7">Rom. viii. 7</reference>. But, alas! the sinner's malice is as impotent as it is impudent; what can he do? <hi type="italic">He strengthens himself</hi> (<hi type="italic">he would be valiant,</hi> so some read it) <hi type="italic">against the Almighty.</hi> He thinks with his exorbitant despotic power to <hi type="italic">change times and laws</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.25">Dan. vii. 25</reference>), and, in spite of Providence, to carry the day for rapine and wrong, clear of the check of conscience. Note, It is the prodigious madness of presumptuous sinners that they enter the lists with Omnipotence. <hi type="italic">Woe unto him that strives with his Maker.</hi> That is generally taken for a further description of the sinner's daring presumption (<reference osisRef="Job.15.26">v. 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">He runs upon him,</hi> upon God himself, in a direct opposition to him, to his precepts and providences, <hi type="italic">even upon his neck,</hi> as a desperate combatant, when he finds himself an unequal match for his adversary, flies in his face, though, at the same time, he falls on his sword's point, or the sharp spike of his buckler. Sinners, in general, run from God; but the presumptuous sinner, who sins with a high hand, runs upon him, fights against him, and bids defiance to him; and it is easy to foretel what will be the issue. [2.] He wraps himself up in security and sensuality (<reference osisRef="Job.15.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">He covers his face with his fatness.</hi> This signifies both the pampering of his flesh with daily delicious fare and the hardening of his heart thereby against the judgments of God. Note, The gratifying of the appetites of the body, feeding and feasting that to the full, often turns to the damage of the soul and its interests. Why is God forgotten and slighted, but because the belly is made a god of and happiness placed in the delights of sense? Those that fill themselves with wine and strong drink abandon all that is serious and flatter themselves with hopes that <hi type="italic">tomorrow shall be as this day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.56.12">Isa. lvi. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">Woe to those that are thus at ease in Zion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.6.1 Amos.6.3 Amos.6.4">Amos vi. 1, 3, 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.12.19">Luke xii. 19</reference>. The fat that covers his face makes him look bold and haughty, and that which covers his flanks makes him lie easy and soft, and feel little; but this will prove poor shelter against the darts of God's wrath. [3.] He enriches himself with the spoils of all about him, <reference osisRef="Job.15.28">v. 28</reference>. He dwells in cities which he himself has made desolate by expelling the inhabitants out of them, that he might be placed alone in them, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.8">Isa. v. 8</reference>. Proud and cruel men take a strange pleasure in ruins, when they are of their own making, in <hi type="italic">destroying cities</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.6">Ps. ix. 6</reference>) and triumphing in the destruction, since they cannot make them their own but by making them <hi type="italic">ready to become heaps,</hi> and frightening the inhabitants out of them. Note, Those that aim to engross the world to themselves, and grasp at all, lose the comfort of all, and make themselves miserable in the midst of all. How does this tyrant gain his point, and make himself master of cities that have all the marks of antiquity upon them? We are told (<reference osisRef="Job.15.35">v. 35</reference>) that he does it by malice and falsehood, the two chief ingredients of <hi type="italic">his</hi> wickedness who was a liar and a murderer from the beginning, <hi type="italic">They conceive mischief,</hi> and then they effect it by <hi type="italic">preparing deceit,</hi> pretending to protect those whom they design to subdue, and making leagues of peace the more effectually to carry on the operations of war. From such wicked men God deliver all good men. <div eID="gen9618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9619" type="x-p"/> (2.) Let us see now what is the miserable condition of this wicked man, both in spiritual and temporal judgments. <div eID="gen9619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9620" type="x-p"/> [1.] His inward peace is continually disturbed. He seems to those about him to be easy, and they therefore envy him and wish themselves in his condition; but he who knows what is in men tells us that a wicked man has so little comfort and satisfaction in his own breast that he is rather to be pitied than envied. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> His own conscience accuses him, and with the pangs and throes of that <hi type="italic">he travaileth in pain all his days,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.15.20">v. 20</reference>. He is continually uneasy at the thought of the cruelties he as been guilty of and the blood in which he has imbrued his hands. His sins stare him in the face at every turn. <hi type="italic">Diri conscia facti mens habet attonitos—Conscious guilt astonishes and confounds. Secondly,</hi> He is vexed at the uncertainty of the continuance of his wealth and power: <hi type="italic">The number of years is hidden to the oppressor.</hi> He knows, whatever he pretends, that they will not last always, and has reason to fear that they will not last long and this he frets at. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> He is under a <hi type="italic">certain fearful expectation of judgment and fiery indignation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.27">Heb. x. 27</reference>), which puts him into, and keeps him in, a continual terror and consternation, so that he dwells with Cain in the land of Nod, or <hi type="italic">commotion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.4.16">Gen. iv. 16</reference>), and is made like, <hi type="italic">Pashur, Magor-missabib—a terror round about,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.20.3-Jer.20.4">Jer. xx. 3, 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">A dreadful sound is in his ears,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.15.21">v. 21</reference>. He knows that both heaven and earth are incensed against him, that God is angry with him and that all the world hates him; he has done nothing to make his peace with either, and therefore he thinks that every one who <hi type="italic">meets him will slay him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.4.14">Gen. iv. 14</reference>. Or he is like a man absconding for debt, who thinks every man a bailiff. Fear came in, at first, with sin (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.10">Gen. iii. 10</reference>) and still attends it. Even in prosperity he is apprehensive that the destroyer will come upon him, either some destroying angel sent of God to avenge his quarrel or some of his injured subjects who will be their own avengers. Those who are the <hi type="italic">terror of the mighty in the land of the living</hi> usually <hi type="italic">go down slain to the pit</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.32.25">Ezek. xxxii. 25</reference>), the expectation of which makes them a terror to themselves. This is further set forth (<reference osisRef="Job.15.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">He is,</hi> in his own apprehension, <hi type="italic">waited for of the sword;</hi> for he knows that <hi type="italic">he who killeth with the sword must be killed with the sword,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.13.10">Rev. xiii. 10</reference>. A guilty conscience represents to the sinner a <hi type="italic">flaming sword turning every way</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.24">Gen. iii. 24</reference>) and himself inevitably running on it. Again (<reference osisRef="Job.15.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">He knows that the day of darkness</hi> (or the <hi type="italic">night</hi> of darkness rather) <hi type="italic">is ready at his hand,</hi> that it is appointed to him and cannot be put by, that it is hastening on apace and cannot be put off. This day of darkness is something beyond death; it is that <hi type="italic">day of the Lord</hi> which to all wicked people will be darkness and not light and in which they will be doomed to utter, endless, darkness. Note, Some wicked people, though they seem secure, have already received the sentence of death, eternal death, within themselves, and plainly see hell gaping for them. No marvel that it follows (<reference osisRef="Job.15.24">v. 24</reference>), <hi type="italic">Trouble and anguish</hi> (that inward tribulation and anguish of soul spoken of <reference osisRef="Rom.2.8-Rom.2.9">Rom. ii. 8, 9</reference>, which are the effect of God's <hi type="italic">indignation and wrath</hi> fastening upon the conscience) <hi type="italic">shall make him afraid</hi> of worse to come. What is the hell before him if this be the hell within him? And though he would fain shake off his fears, drink them away, and jest them away, it will not do; <hi type="italic">they shall prevail against him,</hi> and overpower him, <hi type="italic">as a king ready to the battle,</hi> with forces too strong to be resisted. He that would keep his peace, let him keep a good conscience. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> If at any time he be in trouble, he despairs of getting out (<reference osisRef="Job.15.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">He believeth not that he shall return out of darkness,</hi> but he gives himself up for gone and lost in an endless night. Good men expect <hi type="italic">light at evening time, light out of darkness;</hi> but what reason have those to expect that they shall return out of the darkness of trouble who would not return from the darkness of sin, but <hi type="italic">went on in it?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.82.5">Ps. lxxxii. 5</reference>. It is the misery of damned sinners that they know they shall never return out of that utter darkness, nor pass the gulf there fixed. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> He perplexes himself with continual care, especially if Providence ever so little frown upon him, <reference osisRef="Job.15.23">v. 23</reference>. Such a dread he has of poverty, and such a waste does he discern upon his estate, that he is already, in his own imagination, <hi type="italic">wandering abroad for bread,</hi> going a begging for a meal's meat, and <hi type="italic">saying, Where is it?</hi> The rich man, in his abundance, cried out, <hi type="italic">What shall I do?</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.17">Luke xii. 17</reference>. Perhaps he pretends fear of wanting, as an excuse of his covetous practices; and justly may he be brought to this extremity at last. We read of those who <hi type="italic">were full,</hi> but have <hi type="italic">hired out themselves for bread</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.5">1 Sam. ii. 5</reference>), which this sinner will not do. He cannot dig; he is too fat (<reference osisRef="Job.15.27">v. 27</reference>): but to beg he may well be ashamed. See <reference osisRef="Ps.109.10">Ps. cix. 10</reference>. David never saw the righteous so far forsaken as to beg their bread; for, verily, they shall be fed by the charitable unasked, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.3">Ps. xxxvii. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.25">25</reference>. But the wicked want it, and cannot expect it should be readily given them. How should those find mercy who never showed mercy? <div eID="gen9620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9621" type="x-p"/> [2.] His outward prosperity will soon come to an end, and all his confidence and all his comfort will come to an end with it. How can he prosper when God runs upon him? so some understand that, <reference osisRef="Job.15.26">v. 26</reference>. Whom God runs <hi type="italic">upon</hi> he will certainly run <hi type="italic">down;</hi> for when he judges he will overcome. See how the judgments of God cross this worldly wicked man in all his cares, desires, and projects, and so complete his misery. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He is in care to get, but <hi type="italic">he shall not be rich,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.15.29">v. 29</reference>. His own covetous mind keeps him from being truly rich. He is not rich that has not enough, and he has not enough that does not think he has. It is contentment only that is great gain. Providence remarkably keeps some from being rich, defeating their enterprises, breaking their measures, and keeping them always behind-hand. Many that get much by fraud and injustice, yet do not grow rich: it goes as it comes; it is got by one sin and spent upon another. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He is in care to keep what he has got, but in vain: <hi type="italic">His substance shall not continue;</hi> it will dwindle and come to nothing. God blasts it, and what <hi type="italic">came up in a night perishes in a night. Wealth gotten by vanity will certainly be diminished.</hi> Some have themselves lived to see the ruin of those estates which have been raised by oppression; but, where this is not the case, that which is left goes with a curse to those who succeed. <hi type="italic">De male quæsitis vix gaudet tertius hæres—Ill-gotten property will scarcely be enjoyed by the third generation.</hi> He purchases estates <hi type="italic">to him and his heirs for ever;</hi> but to what purpose? <hi type="italic">He shall not prolong the perfection thereof upon the earth;</hi> neither the credit nor the comfort of his riches shall be prolonged; and, when those are gone, where is the perfection of them? How indeed can we expect the perfection of any thing to be prolonged upon the earth, where every thing is transitory, and we soon see the end of all perfection? <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> He is in care to leave what he has got and kept to his children after him. But in this he is crossed; the branches of his family shall perish, in whom he hoped to live and flourish and to have the reputation of making them all great men. <hi type="italic">They shall not be green,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.15.32">v. 32</reference>. <hi type="italic">The flame shall dry them up,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.15.30">v. 30</reference>. he shall shake them off as blossoms that never knit, or as the <hi type="italic">unripe grape,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.15.33">v. 33</reference>. They shall die in the beginning of their days and never come to maturity. Many a man's family is ruined by his iniquity. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> He is in care to enjoy it a great while himself; but in that also he is crossed. 1. He may perhaps be taken from it (<reference osisRef="Job.15.30">v. 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">By the breath of God's mouth shall he go away,</hi> and leave his wealth to others; that is, by God's wrath, which, <hi type="italic">like a stream of brimstone, kindles</hi> the fire that devours him (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.33">Isa. xxx. 33</reference>), or by his word; he speaks, and it is done immediately. <hi type="italic">This night thy soul shall be required of thee;</hi> and so <hi type="italic">the wicked is driven away in his wickedness,</hi> the worldling in his worldliness. 2. It may perhaps be taken from him, and fly away like an eagle towards heaven: <hi type="italic">It shall be accomplished</hi> (or cut off) <hi type="italic">before his time</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.15.32">v. 32</reference>); that is, he shall survive his prosperity, and see himself stripped of it. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> He is in care, when he is in trouble, how to get out of it (not how to get good by it); but in this also he is crossed (<reference osisRef="Job.15.30">v. 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">He shall not depart out of darkness.</hi> When he begins to fall, like Haman, all men say, "Down with him." It was said of him (<reference osisRef="Job.15.22">v. 22</reference>), <hi type="italic">He believeth not that he shall return out of darkness.</hi> He frightened himself with the perpetuity of his calamity, and God also shall <hi type="italic">choose his delusions</hi> and <hi type="italic">bring his fears upon him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.4">Isa. lxvi. 4</reference>), as he did upon Israel, <reference osisRef="Num.14.28">Num. xiv. 28</reference>. God says <hi type="italic">Amen</hi> to his distrust and despair. <hi type="italic">Sixthly,</hi> He is in care to secure his partners, and hopes to secure himself by his partnership with them; but that is in vain too, <reference osisRef="Job.15.34-Job.15.35">v. 34, 35</reference>. <hi type="italic">The congregation</hi> of them, the whole confederacy, they and all their tabernacles, <hi type="italic">shall be desolate</hi> and consumed with fire. Hypocrisy and bribery are here charged upon them; that is, deceitful dealing both with God and man—God affronted under colour of religion, man wronged under colour of justice. It is impossible that these should end well. <hi type="italic">Though hand join in hand</hi> for the support of these perfidious practices, <hi type="italic">yet shall not the wicked go unpunished.</hi> (3.) The use and application of all this. Will the prosperity of presumptuous sinners end thus miserably? Then (<reference osisRef="Job.15.31">v. 31</reference>) <hi type="italic">let not him that is deceived trust in vanity.</hi> Let the mischiefs which befal others be our warnings, and let not us rest on that broken reed which always failed those who leaned on it. [1.] Those who trust to their sinful ways of getting wealth <hi type="italic">trust in vanity,</hi> and <hi type="italic">vanity will be their recompence,</hi> for they shall not get what they expected. Their arts will deceive them and perhaps ruin them in this world. [2.] Those who trust to their wealth when they have gotten it, especially to the wealth they have gotten dishonestly, trust in vanity; for it will yield them no satisfaction. The guilt that cleaves to it will ruin the joy of it. They sow the wind, and will reap the whirlwind, and will own at length, with the utmost confusion, that <hi type="italic">a deceived heart turned them aside,</hi> and that they cheated themselves with <hi type="italic">a lie in their right hand.</hi>  <chapter eID="Job.15"/> <div eID="gen9621" type="x-p"/>

entries.906910a05dbedc328f249a31d7114828fdda2e83: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4757"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 15</title> <div sID="gen6920" type="x-p"/> SECOND SERIES.<div eID="gen6920" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Job.15.1-Job.15.35">Job 15:1-35</reference>. Second Speech of Eliphaz.</title> <div sID="gen6921" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4757"/><hi type="bold">2. a wise man--</hi>which Job claims to be.<div eID="gen6921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6922" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vain knowledge--</hi>Hebrew, "windy knowledge"; literally, "of wind" (<reference osisRef="Job.8.2">Job 8:2</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.14">Ec 1:14</reference>, Hebrew, "to catch wind," expresses to strive for what is vain.<div eID="gen6922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6923" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">east wind--</hi>stronger than the previous "wind," for in that region the east wind is the most destructive of winds (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.8">Is 27:8</reference>). Thus here,--empty violence.<div eID="gen6923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6924" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">belly--</hi>the inward parts, the breast (<reference osisRef="Prov.18.8">Pr 18:8</reference>). <div eID="gen6924" type="x-p"/>
entries.8886a573bbb4a0171645f0525808623bade8ba1f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4758"/><div sID="gen6925" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4758"/><hi type="bold">4. fear--</hi>reverence for God (<reference osisRef="Job.4.6">Job 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.2.11">Psa 2:11</reference>).<div eID="gen6925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6926" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prayer--</hi>meditation, in <reference osisRef="Ps.104.34">Psa 104:34</reference>; so devotion. If thy views were right, reasons Eliphaz, that God disregards the afflictions of the righteous and makes the wicked to prosper, all devotion would be at an end. <div eID="gen6926" type="x-p"/>

entries.2ed865e982adb9d7da98b35bc50456bd32158156: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4761"/><div sID="gen6929" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4761"/>7. That is, Art thou wisdom personified? Wisdom existed before the hills; that is, the eternal Son of God (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.25">Pr 8:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.90.2">Psa 90:2</reference>). Wast thou in existence before Adam? The farther back one existed, the nearer he was to the Eternal Wisdom. <div eID="gen6929" type="x-p"/>
entries.823081c03bc434456aaeff11784fcd7308791c74: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4762"/><div sID="gen6930" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4762"/><hi type="bold">8. secret--</hi>rather, "Wast thou a listener in the secret council of God?" The Hebrew means properly the cushions of a divan on which counsellors in the East usually sit. God's servants are admitted to God's secrets (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.14">Psa 25:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.18.17">Ge 18:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.15.15">Joh 15:15</reference>).<div eID="gen6930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6931" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">restrain--</hi>Rather, didst thou take away, or borrow, thence (namely, from the divine secret council) thy wisdom? Eliphaz in this (<reference osisRef="Job.15.8">Job 15:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.15.9">9</reference>) retorts Job's words upon himself (<reference osisRef="Job.12.2">Job 12:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.12.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.13.2">13:2</reference>). <div eID="gen6931" type="x-p"/>
entries.637de11d46adf24f4d87068461630f645e6a2511: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4763"/><div sID="gen6932" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4763"/><hi type="bold">9. in us--</hi>or, "with us," Hebraism for "we are aware of." <div eID="gen6932" type="x-p"/>
entries.fa3871f4bae8dc69f70c469d30fcf86b779fbf52: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4764"/><div sID="gen6933" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4764"/>10. On our side, thinking with us are the aged. Job had admitted that wisdom is with them (<reference osisRef="Job.12.12">Job 12:12</reference>). Eliphaz seems to have been himself older than Job; perhaps the other two were also (<reference osisRef="Job.32.6">Job 32:6</reference>). Job, in <reference osisRef="Job.30.1">Job 30:1</reference>, does not refer to his three friends; it therefore forms no objection. The Arabs are proud of fulness of years. <div eID="gen6933" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e7048269e457fbac614c6559255861c843e6ffa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4765"/><div sID="gen6934" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4765"/><hi type="bold">11. consolations--</hi>namely, the revelation which Eliphaz had stated as a consolatory reproof to Job, and which he repeats in <reference osisRef="Job.15.14">Job 15:14</reference>.<div eID="gen6934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6935" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">secret--</hi>Hast thou some secret wisdom and source of consolation, which makes thee disregard those suggested by me? (<reference osisRef="Job.15.8">Job 15:8</reference>). Rather, from a different Hebrew root, Is the word of kindness or gentleness addressed by me treated by thee as valueless? [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen6935" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a76e1d7bfe14f711497f0f507e51ea5f9fcf3bf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4766"/><div sID="gen6936" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4766"/><hi type="bold">12. wink--</hi>that is, why do thy eyes evince pride? (<reference osisRef="Prov.6.13">Pr 6:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.35.19">Psa 35:19</reference>). <div eID="gen6936" type="x-p"/>
entries.4acc4247247b8b0a1851ba96102ff1722ccfe4c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4767"/><div sID="gen6937" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4767"/>13. That is, frettest against God and lettest fall rash words. <div eID="gen6937" type="x-p"/>
entries.62f29eeec28e205ee3234d2e100dc10e1ee962b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4768"/><div sID="gen6938" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4768"/>14. Eliphaz repeats the revelation (<reference osisRef="Job.4.17">Job 4:17</reference>) in substance, but using Job's own words (see on <reference osisRef="Job.14.1">Job 14:1</reference>, on "born of a woman") to strike him with his own weapons. <div eID="gen6938" type="x-p"/>
entries.61fb71225bde93e8848ef9c564b7d2af5707bbd7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4769"/><div sID="gen6939" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4769"/>15. Repeated from <reference osisRef="Job.4.18">Job 4:18</reference>; "servants" there are "saints" here; namely, holy angels.<div eID="gen6939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6940" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heavens--</hi>literally, or else answering to "angels" (see on <reference osisRef="Job.4.18">Job 4:18</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Job.25.5">Job 25:5</reference>). <div eID="gen6940" type="x-p"/>
entries.9f5c35313b0aafd297040d5d930665bc9694bed8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4770"/><div sID="gen6941" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4770"/><hi type="bold">16. filthy--</hi>in Arabic "sour" (<reference osisRef="Ps.14.3">Psa 14:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.53.3">53:3</reference>), corrupted from his original purity.<div eID="gen6941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6942" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">drinketh--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.19.28">Pr 19:28</reference>). <div eID="gen6942" type="x-p"/>
entries.f7b4a77eefc56f281383aa7f70e5bb123e1fcc89: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4771"/><div sID="gen6943" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4771"/>17. In direct contradiction of Job's position (<reference osisRef="Job.12.6">Job 12:6</reference>, &c.), that the lot of the wicked was the most prosperous here, Eliphaz appeals (1) to his own experience, (2) to the wisdom of the ancients. <div eID="gen6943" type="x-p"/>
entries.e2dbbb08b6b950a2096a1abc725e3ec7aa4f7000: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4772"/><div sID="gen6944" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4772"/>18. Rather, "and which as handed down from their fathers, they have not concealed." <div eID="gen6944" type="x-p"/>
entries.58560a4a026e4eaf83bbe538e2f233d4cbd42fda: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4773"/><div sID="gen6945" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4773"/>19. Eliphaz speaks like a genuine Arab when he boasts that his ancestors had ever possessed the land unmixed with foreigners [Umbreit]. His words are intended to oppose Job's (<reference osisRef="Job.9.24">Job 9:24</reference>); "the earth" in their case was not "given into the hand of the wicked." He refers to the division of the earth by divine appointment (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.5">Ge 10:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.25.32">25:32</reference>). Also he may insinuate that Job's sentiments had been corrupted from original purity by his vicinity to the Sabeans and Chaldeans [Rosenmuller]. <div eID="gen6945" type="x-p"/>
entries.d4a15f20609d087d9fe058325044f8eb47ab8bd3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4774"/><div sID="gen6946" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4774"/><hi type="bold">20. travaileth--</hi>rather, "trembleth of himself," though there is no real danger [Umbreit].<div eID="gen6946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6947" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the number of his years, &c.--</hi>This gives the reason why the wicked man trembles continually; namely, because he knows not the moment when his life must end. <div eID="gen6947" type="x-p"/>
entries.0ee5c7de55a4af8a7cb33b206f665750091ac160: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4775"/><div sID="gen6948" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4775"/>21. An evil conscience conceives alarm at every sudden sound, though it be in a time of peace ("prosperity"), when there is no real danger (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.36">Le 26:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.28.1">Pr 28:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.7.6">2Ki 7:6</reference>). <div eID="gen6948" type="x-p"/>
entries.b1d2e2c25897bf631e41be511f04f15636d4d859: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4776"/><div sID="gen6949" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4776"/><hi type="bold">22. darkness--</hi>namely, danger or calamity. Glancing at Job, who despaired of restoration: in contrast to good men when in darkness (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.8">Mi 7:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.9">9</reference>).<div eID="gen6949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6950" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">waited for of--</hi>that is, He is destined for the sword [Gesenius]. Rather (in the night of danger), "he looks anxiously towards the sword," as if every sword was drawn against him [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen6950" type="x-p"/>
entries.acd4c7ffe83a72f3e60f95c43720d9c11fa706ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4777"/><div sID="gen6951" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4777"/>23. Wandereth in anxious search for bread. Famine in Old Testament depicts sore need (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.13">Is 5:13</reference>). Contrast the pious man's lot (<reference osisRef="Job.5.20-Job.5.22">Job 5:20-22</reference>).<div eID="gen6951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6952" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knoweth--</hi>has the firm conviction. Contrast the same word applied to the pious (<reference osisRef="Job.5.24">Job 5:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.5.25">25</reference>).<div eID="gen6952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6953" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ready at his hand--</hi>an Arabic phrase to denote a thing's complete readiness and full presence, as if in the hand. <div eID="gen6953" type="x-p"/>
entries.ee82a59064abcd32e7533643080299dcdc042808: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4778"/><div sID="gen6954" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4778"/><hi type="bold">24. prevail--</hi>break upon him suddenly and terribly, as a king, &c. (<reference osisRef="Prov.6.11">Pr 6:11</reference>). <div eID="gen6954" type="x-p"/>
entries.c6bfd6f54d64d0d6381712ffa08d96342c7b9d59: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4779"/><div sID="gen6955" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4779"/><hi type="bold">25. stretcheth ... hand--</hi>wielding the spear, as a bold rebel against God (<reference osisRef="Job.9.4">Job 9:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.27.4">Is 27:4</reference>). <div eID="gen6955" type="x-p"/>
entries.fda35224f0a47ab13fccb8e2966ec3debdfa3bc0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4780"/><div sID="gen6956" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4780"/><hi type="bold">26. on his neck--</hi>rather, "with outstretched neck," namely, that of the rebel [Umbreit] (<reference osisRef="Ps.75.5">Psa 75:5</reference>).<div eID="gen6956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6957" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon ... bucklers--</hi>rather, "with--his (the rebel's, not God's) bucklers." The rebel and his fellows are depicted as joining shields together, to form a compact covering over their heads against the weapons hurled on them from a fortress [Umbreit and Gesenius]. <div eID="gen6957" type="x-p"/>
entries.4408b21a4650bf22701e309a4d662fa7e6bfdff9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4781"/><div sID="gen6958" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4781"/>27. The well-nourished body of the rebel is the sign of his prosperity.<div eID="gen6958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6959" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">collops--</hi>masses of fat. He pampers and fattens himself with sensual indulgences; hence his rebellion against God (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.15">De 32:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.29">1Sa 2:29</reference>). <div eID="gen6959" type="x-p"/>
entries.143706bfa3c5d4bfa14c9abf3b2c2109d1251cd2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4782"/><div sID="gen6960" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4782"/>28. The class of wicked here described is that of robbers who plunder "cities," and seize on the houses of the banished citizens (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.20">Is 13:20</reference>). Eliphaz chooses this class because Job had chosen the same (<reference osisRef="Job.12.6">Job 12:6</reference>).<div eID="gen6960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6961" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heaps--</hi>of ruins. <div eID="gen6961" type="x-p"/>
entries.8fee8b8707497fe42206043e38a2fc3e9d2ed960: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4783"/><div sID="gen6962" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4783"/>29. Rather, he shall not increase his riches; he has reached his highest point; his prosperity shall not continue.<div eID="gen6962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6963" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">perfection--</hi>rather, "His acquired wealth--what he possesses--shall not be extended," &c. <div eID="gen6963" type="x-p"/>
entries.2252516a11ee609a40d09a25f55e1d389f8ce8a4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4784"/><div sID="gen6964" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4784"/><hi type="bold">30. depart--</hi>that is, escape (<reference osisRef="Job.15.22">Job 15:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.15.23">23</reference>).<div eID="gen6964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6965" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">branches--</hi>namely, his offspring (<reference osisRef="Job.1.18">Job 1:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.19">19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.37.35">Psa 37:35</reference>).<div eID="gen6965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6966" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dry up--</hi>The "flame" is the sultry wind in the East by which plants most full of sap are suddenly shrivelled.<div eID="gen6966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6967" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his mouth--</hi>that is, God's wrath (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">Is 11:4</reference>). <div eID="gen6967" type="x-p"/>
entries.464dda3ce05d4fe24ee52fb3e6b5a6bc0e2f8503: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4785"/><div sID="gen6968" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4785"/>31. Rather, "let him not trust in vanity or he will be deceived," &c.<div eID="gen6968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6969" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vanity--</hi>that which is unsubstantial. Sin is its own punishment (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.31">Pr 1:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.19">Jr 2:19</reference>). <div eID="gen6969" type="x-p"/>
entries.df8b6b7f828ebaa73f088250cbacbf3eba8ddc2c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4786"/><div sID="gen6970" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4786"/>32. Literally, "it (the tree to which he is compared, <reference osisRef="Job.15.30">Job 15:30</reference>, or else his life) shall not be filled up in its time"; that is, "he shall be ended before his time."<div eID="gen6970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6971" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall not be green--</hi>image from a withered tree; the childless extinction of the wicked. <div eID="gen6971" type="x-p"/>
entries.afb78539b5f3aadbdbee396ba8e44fb18698f82b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4787"/><div sID="gen6972" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4787"/>33. Images of incompleteness. The loss of the unripe grapes is poetically made the vine tree's own act, in order to express more pointedly that the sinner's ruin is the fruit of his own conduct (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.11">Is 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.19">Jr 6:19</reference>). <div eID="gen6972" type="x-p"/>
entries.31330095753f7249a31ad85eabdd22fe07715aef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4788"/><div sID="gen6973" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4788"/>34. Rather, The binding together of the hypocrites (wicked) shall be fruitless [Umbreit].<div eID="gen6973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6974" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tabernacles of bribery--</hi>namely, dwellings of unjust judges, often reprobated in the Old Testament (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.23">Is 1:23</reference>). The "fire of God" that consumed Job's possessions (<reference osisRef="Job.1.16">Job 1:16</reference>) Eliphaz insinuates may have been on account of Job's bribery as an Arab sheik or emir. <div eID="gen6974" type="x-p"/>
entries.33209702118bf85d8c9f2f687c2875472b927d72: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4789"/><div sID="gen6975" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4789"/>35. Bitter irony, illustrating the "unfruitfulness" (<reference osisRef="Job.15.34">Job 15:34</reference>) of the wicked. Their conceptions and birthgivings consist solely in mischief, &c. (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.11">Is 33:11</reference>).<div eID="gen6975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6976" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prepareth--</hi>hatcheth. <chapter eID="Job.15"/>

entries.959f99300ebc175472d373278ea7b710fac9460e: <div eID="gen16545" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen16546" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16547" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16547" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16546" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16548" type="x-p"/> Eliphaz charges Job with impiety in attempting to justify himself, <reference osisRef="Job.15.1-Job.15.13">Job 15:1-13</reference>; asserts the utter corruption and abominable state of man, <reference osisRef="Job.15.14-Job.15.16">Job 15:14-16</reference>; and, from his own knowledge and the observations of the ancients, shows the desolation to which the wicked are exposed, and insinuates that Job has such calamities to dread, vv. 17-35.
entries.49998a8df3a6c91f809e85cefc0ab225e7fce840: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen16548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16549" type="x-p"/> Should a wise man utter vain knowledge - Or rather, Should a wise man utter the science of wind? A science without solidity or certainty. <div eID="gen16549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16550" type="x-p"/> And fill his belly with the east wind? - בטן beten, which we translate belly, is used to signify any part of the cavity of the body, whether the region of the thorax or abdomen; here it evidently refers to the lungs, and may include the cheeks and fauces. The east wind, קדים kadim, is a very stormy wind in the Levant, or the eastern part of the Mediterranean Sea, supposed to be the same with that called by the Greeks ευροκλυδων, euroclydon, the east storm, mentioned <reference osisRef="Act.27.14">Act 27:14</reference>. Eliphaz, by these words, seems to intimate that Job's speech was a perfect storm or tempest of words.
entries.05d29458f05ebcfa9f74975fede6764dab1b72b2: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen16550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16551" type="x-p"/> Should he reason with unprofitable talk? - Should a man talk disrespectfully of his Maker, or speak to him without reverence? and should he suppose that he has proved any thing, when he has uttered words of little meaning, and used sound instead of sense?
entries.2e59f4279358c2f0de0ed237fa9d6bf1da464aad: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen16551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16552" type="x-p"/> Thou castest off fear - Thou hast no reverence for God. <div eID="gen16552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16553" type="x-p"/> And restrainest prayer - Instead of humbling thyself, and making supplication to thy Judge, thou spendest thy time in arraigning his providence and justifying thyself. When a man has any doubts whether he has grieved God's Spirit, and his mind feels troubled, it is much better for him to go immediately to God, and ask forgiveness, than spend any time in finding excuses for his conduct, or laboring to divest it of its seeming obliquity. Restraining or suppressing prayer, in order to find excuses or palliations for infirmities, indiscretions, or improprieties of any kind, which appear to trench on the sacred limits of morality and godliness, may be to a man the worst of evils: humiliation and prayer for mercy and pardon can never be out of their place to any soul of man who, surrounded with evils, is ever liable to offend.
entries.d87453858d6bd7058ee9c18d4e81f7c0b469dd1f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen16553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16554" type="x-p"/> For thy mouth uttereth - In attempting to justify thyself, thou hast added iniquity to sin, and hast endeavored to impute blame to thy Maker. <div eID="gen16554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16555" type="x-p"/> The tongue of the crafty - Thou hast varnished thy own conduct, and used sophistical arguments to defend thyself. Thou resemblest those cunning persons, ערומים arumim, who derive their skill and dexterity from the old serpent, "the nachash, who was ערום arum, subtle, or crafty, beyond all the beasts of the field;" <reference osisRef="Gen.3.1">Gen 3:1</reference>. Thy wisdom is not from above, but from beneath.
entries.9d534a3dbfa31cee1e56f9b0597a54017f73b021: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen16555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16556" type="x-p"/> Art thou the first man that was born? - Literally, "Wert thou born before Adam?" Art thou in the pristine state of purity and innocence? Or art thou like Adam in his first state? It does not become the fallen descendant of a fallen parent to talk as thou dost. <div eID="gen16556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16557" type="x-p"/> Made before the hills? - Did God create thee the beginning of his ways? or wert thou the first intelligent creature which his hands have formed?
entries.5053ad450c70e4d417ef02af9b0a686f92855e6c: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen16557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16558" type="x-p"/> Hast thou heard the secret of God? - "Hast thou hearkened in God's council?" Wert thou one of the celestial cabinet, when God said, Let Us make man in Our image, and in Our likeness? <div eID="gen16558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16559" type="x-p"/> Dost thou restrain wisdom to thyself? - Dost thou wish us to understand that God's counsels were revealed to none but thyself? And dost thou desire that we should give implicit credence to whatsoever thou art pleased to speak? These are all strong sarcastic questions, and apparently uttered with great contempt.
entries.45dcaae50e4c98d942d742ae142d5156968ae514: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen16559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16560" type="x-p"/> What knowest thou - Is it likely that thy intellect is greater than ours; and that thou hast cultivated it better than we have done ours? <div eID="gen16560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16561" type="x-p"/> What understandest thou - Or, Dost thou understand any thing, and it is not with us? Show us any point of knowledge possessed by thyself, of which we are ignorant.
entries.f5920c01c6db79684498dd6f3bf60d2ed07eddc6: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen16561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16562" type="x-p"/> With us are both the gray-headed - One copy of the Chaldee Targum paraphrases the verse thus: "Truly Eliphaz the hoary-headed, and Bildad the long-lived, are among us; and Zophar, who in age surpasseth thy father." It is very likely that Eliphaz refers to himself and his friends in this verse, and not either to the old men of their tribes, or to the masters by whom they themselves were instructed. Eliphaz seems to have been the eldest of these sages; and, therefore, he takes the lead in each part of this dramatic poem.
entries.ee53f5f5ab492f2ef662f98781c921719b0ff3b4: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen16562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16563" type="x-p"/> Are the consolations of God small with thee? - Various are the renderings of this verse. Mr. Good translates the verse thus: "Are then the mercies of God of no account with thee?" or, "the addresses of kindness before thee?" <div eID="gen16563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16564" type="x-p"/> The Vulgate thus: - "Can it be a difficult thing for God to comfort thee? But thou hinderest this by thy intemperate speeches." <div eID="gen16564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16565" type="x-p"/> The Syriac and Arabic thus: - "Remove from thee the threatenings (Arabic, reproaches) of God, and speak tranquilly with thy own spirit." <div eID="gen16565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16566" type="x-p"/> The Septuagint thus: - "Thou hast been scourged lightly for the sins which thou hast committed; and thou hast spoken greatly beyond measure; or, with excessive insolence." <div eID="gen16566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16567" type="x-p"/> Houbigant thus: - "Dost thou not regard the threatenings of God; or, has there been any thing darkly revealed to thee." <div eID="gen16567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16568" type="x-p"/> Coverdale: - Dost thou no more regarde the comforte of God? But thy wicked wordes wil not suffre the. <div eID="gen16568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16569" type="x-p"/> Scarcely any two translators or interpreters agree in the translation, or even meaning of this verse. The sense, as expressed in the Vulgate, or in our own version, or that of Coverdale, is plain enough: - "Hast thou been so unfaithful to God, that he has withdrawn his consolations from thy heart? And is there any secret thing, any bosom sin, which thou wilt not give up, that has thus provoked thy Maker?" This is the sense of our version: and I believe it to be as near the original as any yet offered. I may just add the Chaldee - "Are the consolations of God few to thee? And has a word in secret been spoken unto thee?" And I shall close all these with the Hebrew text, and the literal version of Arius Montanus: - המעט ממך ינחומות אל hameat mimmecha tanchumoth el. ודבר לאט עמך vedabar laat immak. <div eID="gen16569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16570" type="x-p"/> Nonne parum a te consolationes Dei? Et verbum latet tecum? "Are not the consolations of God small to thee? And does a word (or thing) lie hidden with thee?" <div eID="gen16570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16571" type="x-p"/> Now, let the reader choose for himself.
entries.bd7e2bbcdb0da95a653299252614d688a3271605: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen16571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16572" type="x-p"/> Why doth thine heart carry thee away? - Why is it that thou dost conceive and entertain such high sentiments of thyself? <div eID="gen16572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16573" type="x-p"/> And what do thy eyes wink at - With what splendid opinion of thyself is thine eye dazzled?
