Perhaps there is an allusion here to that sparkling in the eye which is excited by sensations of joy and pleasing objects of sight, or to that furious rolling of the eyes observed in deranged persons. Rosenmuller translates thus: - <div eID="gen16573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16574" type="x-p"/> Quo te tuus animus rapit? <div eID="gen16574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16575" type="x-p"/> Quid occuli tui vibrantes? "Whither does thy soul hurry thee? <div eID="gen16575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16576" type="x-p"/> What mean thy rolling eyes?" <div eID="gen16576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16577" type="x-p"/> Thou seemest transported beyond thyself; thou art actuated by a furious spirit. Thou art beside thyself; thy words and thy eyes show it. None but a madman could speak and act as thou dost; for thou turnest thy spirit against God, and lettest such words go out of thy mouth, <reference osisRef="Job.15.13">Job 15:13</reference>. This latter sense seems to agree best with the words of the text, and with the context.
entries.980d6f4ab83fe5062fb39e77d5972299dfd5fa86: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen16577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16578" type="x-p"/> That thou turnest thy spirit against God - The ideas here seem to be taken from an archer, who turns his eye and his spirit - his desire - against the object which he wishes to hit; and then lets loose his arrow that it may attain the mark.
entries.4663bae3242aa2507c140ae17245d7c3c13d7f8a: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen16578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16579" type="x-p"/> What is man, that he should be clean? - מה אנוש mah enosh; what is weak, sickly, dying, miserable man, that he should be clean? This is the import of the original word enosh. <div eID="gen16579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16580" type="x-p"/> And - born of a woman, that he should be righteous? - It appears, from many passages in the sacred writings, that natural birth was supposed to be a defilement; and that every man born into the world was in a state of moral pollution. Perhaps the word יצדק yitsdak should be translated, that he should justify himself, and not that he should be righteous.
entries.e92c5b43593cb5010bba6a86562b13b406aab66e: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen16580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16581" type="x-p"/> Behold, he putteth no trust in his saints; yea, the heavens are not clean in his sight - The Vulgate has, "Behold, among his saints, none is immutable; and the heavens are not clean in his sight." <div eID="gen16581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16582" type="x-p"/> Coverdale - Beholde, he hath found unfaithfulnesse amonge his owne sanctes, yea the very heavens are unclene in his sight. <div eID="gen16582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16583" type="x-p"/> Eliphaz uses the same mode of speech, <reference osisRef="Job.4.17-Job.4.18">Job 4:17-18</reference> (note); where see the notes. Nothing is immutable but God: saints may fall; angels may fall; all their goodness is derived and dependent. The heavens themselves have no purity compared with his.
entries.18cf8432ce6dc00a912bdf2fd8836f90576a4df8: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen16583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16584" type="x-p"/> How much more abominable and filthy is man - As in the preceding verse it is said, he putteth no trust in his saints, it has appeared both to translators and commentators that the original words, אף כי aph ki, should be rendered how much Less, not how much More: How much less would he put confidence in man, who is filthy and abominable in his natures and profligate in his practice, as he drinks down iniquity like water? A man who is under the power of sinful propensities commits sin as greedily as the thirsty man or camel drinks down water. He thinks he can never have enough. This is a finished character of a Bad man; he hungers and thirsts after Sin: on the contrary, the Good man hungers and thirsts after Righteousness.
entries.233dd13595f50c141ff1c4248026988f3a00c9ba: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen16584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16585" type="x-p"/> I will show thee, hear me; and that which I have seen I will declare - Eliphaz is now about to quote a whole collection of wise sayings from the ancients; all good enough in themselves, but sinfully misapplied to the case of Job.
entries.4a81fa85a758a94fd9c2a1fff3cf1a781b3f5dd3: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen16585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16586" type="x-p"/> Unto whom alone the earth was given - He very likely refers to the Israelites, who got possession of the promised land from God himself; no stranger being permitted to dwell in it, as the old inhabitants were to be exterminated. Some think that Noah and his sons may be intended; as it is certain that the whole earth was given to them, when there were no strangers - no other family of mankind - in being. But, system apart, the words seem to apply more clearly to the Israelites.
entries.ccec331b8cd3428543eb3773a5f3cf03633976fe: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen16586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16587" type="x-p"/> The wicked man travaileth with pain - This is a most forcible truth: a life of sin is a life of misery; and he that Will sin Must suffer. One of the Targums gives it a strange turn: - "All the days of the ungodly Esau, he was expected to repent, but he did not repent; and the number of years was hidden from the sturdy Ishmael." The sense of the original, מתחולל mithcholel, is he torments himself: he is a true heautontimoreumenos, or self-tormentor; and he alone is author of his own sufferings, and of his own ruin.
entries.01587a94092b1dc785e87405604addbe189c57f9: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen16587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16588" type="x-p"/> A dreadful sound is in his ears - If he be an oppressor or tyrant, he can have no rest: he is full of suspicions that the cruelties he has exercised on others shall be one day exercised on himself; for even in his prosperity he may expect the destroyer to rush upon him.
entries.a18c10585955f716b5d4b6c58a2d1a7f791a8709: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen16588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16589" type="x-p"/> That he shall return out of darkness - If he take but a few steps in the dark, he expects the dagger of the assassin. This appears to be the only meaning of the place. Some think the passage should be understood to signify that he has no hope of a resurrection; he can never escape from the tomb. This I doubt: in the days of the writer of this book, the doctrine of a future judgment was understood in every part of the East where the knowledge of the true God was diffused.
entries.9fbc0486fa8dd8d278894044ce2def5523004499: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen16589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16590" type="x-p"/> He wandereth abroad for bread - He is reduced to a state of the utmost indigence, he who was once in affluence requires a morsel of bread, and can scarcely by begging procure enough to sustain life. <div eID="gen16590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16591" type="x-p"/> Is ready at his hand - Is בידו beyado, in his hand - in his possession. As he cannot get bread, he must soon meet death.
entries.e6485f5e2d305a262bd16c554ef07f78a9712a47: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen16591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16592" type="x-p"/> Trouble and anguish shall make him afraid - He shall be in continual fear of death; being now brought down by adversity, and stripped of all the goods which he had got by oppression, his life is a mark for the meanest assassin. <div eID="gen16592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16593" type="x-p"/> As a king ready to the battle - The acts of his wickedness and oppression are as numerous as the troops he commands; and when he comes to meet his enemy in the field, he is not only deserted but slain by his troops. How true are the words of the poet: - <div eID="gen16593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16594" type="x-p"/> Ad generum Cereris sine caede et vulnere pauci <div eID="gen16594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16595" type="x-p"/> Descendunt reges, et sicca morte tyranni. <div eID="gen16595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16596" type="x-p"/> Juv. Sat., ver. 112. "For few usurpers to the shades descend <div eID="gen16596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16597" type="x-p"/> By a dry death, or with a quiet end."
entries.4edbe9d33f85b60afffbbb32ae28338a860547a8: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen16597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16598" type="x-p"/> He stretcheth out his hand against God - While in power he thought himself supreme. He not only did not acknowledge God, by whom kings reign, but stretched out his hand - used his power, not to protect, but to oppress those over whom he had supreme rule; and thus strengthened himself against the Almighty.
entries.d3e6d4ae30689201e5b038d035bfdf8cb1c928e2: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen16598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16599" type="x-p"/> He runneth upon him - Calmet has properly observed that this refers to God, who, like a mighty conquering hero, marches against the ungodly, rushes upon him, seizes him by the throat, which the mail by which it is encompassed cannot protect; neither his shield nor spear can save him when the Lord of hosts comes against him.
entries.4ed1737d2c8c20edeec93115530f01a168070f8b: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen16599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16600" type="x-p"/> Because he covereth his face - He has lived in luxury and excess; and like a man overloaded with flesh, he cannot defend himself against the strong gripe of his adversary. The Arabic, for maketh collops of fat on his flanks, has (Arabic) He lays the Pleiades upon the Hyades, or, He places Surreea upon aiyuk, a proverbial expression for, His ambition is boundless; He aspires as high as heaven; His head touches the stars; or, is like the giants of old, who were fabled to have attempted to scale heaven by placing one high mountain upon another: - <div eID="gen16600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16601" type="x-p"/> Ter sunt conati imponere Pelio Ossam <div eID="gen16601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16602" type="x-p"/> Scilicet, atque Ossae frondosum involvere Olympum <div eID="gen16602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16603" type="x-p"/> Ter Pater extructos disjecit fulmine montes. <div eID="gen16603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16604" type="x-p"/> Virg. Geor. i., ver. 281. "With mountains piled on mountains, thrice they strove <div eID="gen16604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16605" type="x-p"/> To scale the steepy battlements of Jove; <div eID="gen16605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16606" type="x-p"/> And thrice his lightning and red thunder play'd, <div eID="gen16606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16607" type="x-p"/> And their demolished works in ruins laid." <div eID="gen16607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16608" type="x-p"/> Dryden. <div eID="gen16608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16609" type="x-p"/> To the lust of power and the schemes of ambition there are no bounds; but see the end of such persons: the haughty spirit precedes a fall; their palaces become desolate; and their heaven is reduced to a chaos.
entries.e51616fd4e0a2768fc4fc888f7ce1b9dbaee1bd9: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen16609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16610" type="x-p"/> He dwelleth in desolate cities - It is sometimes the fate of a tyrant to be obliged to take up his habitation in some of those cities which have been ruined by his wars, and in a house so ruinous as to be ready to fall into heaps. Ancient and modern history afford abundance of examples to illustrate this.
entries.d7a13e99cf19d819b4cb2ba16a476f747bd02819: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen16610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16611" type="x-p"/> He shall not be rich - The whole of what follows, to the end of the chapter, seems to be directed against Job himself, whom Eliphaz indirectly accuses of having been a tyrant and oppressor. The threatened evils are, <div eID="gen16611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16612" type="x-p"/> 1. He shall not be rich, though he labors greatly to acquire riches. <div eID="gen16612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16613" type="x-p"/> 2. His substance shall not continue - God will blast it, and deprive him of power to preserve it. <div eID="gen16613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16614" type="x-p"/> 3. Neither shall he prolong the perfection thereof - all his works shall perish, for God will blot out his remembrance from under heaven.
entries.bfd8ddb6b6b91519a29732e3f1a06b3ae846b5a1: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen16614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16615" type="x-p"/> He shall not depart out of darkness - <div eID="gen16615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16616" type="x-p"/> 4. He shall be in continual afflictions and distress. <div eID="gen16616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16617" type="x-p"/> 5. The flame shall dry up his branches - his children shall be cut off by sudden judgments. <div eID="gen16617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16618" type="x-p"/> 6. He shall pass away by the breath of his mouth; for by the breath of his mouth doth God slay the wicked.
entries.08c2640fea1ade230824c8ca4c36a5c3b5518753: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen16618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16619" type="x-p"/> Let not him that is deceived - <div eID="gen16619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16620" type="x-p"/> 7. He has many vain imaginations of obtaining wealth, power, pleasure, and happiness; but he is deceived; and he finds that he has trusted בשוא bashshav, in a lie; and this lie is his recompense.
entries.9e66264184eb69e2a5e2c5c3dac2704aebe94df1: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen16620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16621" type="x-p"/> It shall be accomplished before his time - I believe the Vulgate gives the true sense: Antequam dies ejus impleantur, peribit; "He shall perish before his time; before his days are completed." <div eID="gen16621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16622" type="x-p"/> 8. He shall be removed by a violent death, and not live out half his days. <div eID="gen16622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16623" type="x-p"/> 9. And his branch shall not be green - there shall be no scion from his roots; all his posterity shall fail.
entries.c8392f8404125d6baf7b4fede4029c03b41e3130: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen16623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16624" type="x-p"/> He shall shake off his unripe grape - <div eID="gen16624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16625" type="x-p"/> 10. Whatever children he may have, they shall never survive him, nor come to mature age. They shall be like wind-fall grapes and blasted olive blossoms. As the vine and olive, which are among the most useful trees, affording wine and oil, so necessary for the worship of God and the comfort of man, are mentioned here, they may be intended to refer to the hopeful progeny of the oppressor; but who fell, like the untimely grape or the blasted olive flower, without having the opportunity of realizing the public expectation.
entries.8e3c458d3b2f39a6fbce8ddc014463b4c74a611a: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen16625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16626" type="x-p"/> The congregation of hypocrites - <div eID="gen16626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16627" type="x-p"/> 11. Job is here classed with hypocrites, or rather the impious of all kinds. The congregation, or עדת adath, society, of such, shall be desolate, or a barren rock, גלמוד galmud. See this Arabic word explained in the note on <reference osisRef="Job.3.7">Job 3:7</reference> (note). <div eID="gen16627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16628" type="x-p"/> Fire shall consume the tabernacles of bribery - <div eID="gen16628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16629" type="x-p"/> 12. Another insinuation against Job, that he had perverted justice and judgment, and had taken bribes.
entries.f3c2fa1349684e284c67caa0167eb74d3ebd5253: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen16629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16630" type="x-p"/> They conceive mischief - The figure here is both elegant and impressive. The wicked conceive mischief, from the seed which Satan sows in their hearts; in producing which they travail with many pangs, (for sin is a sore labor), and at last their womb produces fraud or deception. This is an accursed birth, from an iniquitous conception. St. James gives the figure at full length, most beautifully touched in all its parts: When lust hath conceived it bringeth forth sin; and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death; <reference osisRef="Jam.1.15">Jam 1:15</reference> (note), where see the note. Poor Job! what a fight of affliction had he to contend with! His body wasted and tortured with sore disease; his mind harassed by Satan; and his heart wrung with the unkindness, and false accusations of his friends. No wonder he was greatly agitated, often distracted, and sometimes even thrown off his guard. However, all his enemies were chained; and beyond that chain they could not go. God was his unseen Protector, and did not suffer his faithful servant to be greatly moved.  <chapter eID="Job.15"/> <div eID="gen16630" type="x-p"/>

entries.3199ada0ca82b78a7cf2985d5a15e6a3a51484a7: <reference osisRef="Job.15.1-Job.6.1">Job 15:1-6   1</reference>  Then began Eliphaz the Temanite, and said:   2  Doth a wise man utter vain knowledge, <div eID="gen7457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7458" type="x-p"/> And fill his breast with the east wind?   3  Contending with words, that profit not, <div eID="gen7458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7459" type="x-p"/> And speeches, by which no good is done?   4  Moreover, thou makest void the fear of God, <div eID="gen7459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7460" type="x-p"/> And thou restrainest devotion before God;   5  For thy mouth exposeth thy misdeeds, <div eID="gen7460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7461" type="x-p"/> And thou choosest the language of the crafty.   6  Thine own mouth condemneth thee and not I, <div eID="gen7461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7462" type="x-p"/> And thine own lips testify against thee. <div eID="gen7462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7463" type="x-p"/> The second course of the controversy is again opened by Eliphaz, the most respectable, most influential, and perhaps oldest of the friends. Job’s detailed and bitter answers seem to him as empty words and impassioned tirades, which ill become a wise man, such as he claims to be in assertions like <reference osisRef="Job.12.3">Job 12:3</reference>; Job 13:2. החלם with <hi type="italic">He interr.</hi>, like העלה, Job 13:25. רוּח, wind, is the opposite of what is solid and sure; and קדים in the parallel (like Hos 12:2) signifies what is worthless, with the additional notion of vehement action. If we translate בּטן by “belly,” the meaning is apt to be misunderstood; it is not intended as the opposite of לב fo et (Ewald), but it means, especially in the book of Job, not only that which feels, but also thinks and wills, the spiritually receptive and active inner nature of man (<hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 266); as also in Arabic, <hi type="italic">el - battin</hi> signifies that which is within, in the deepest mystical sense. Hirz. and Renan translate the <hi type="italic">inf. abs.</hi> הוכח, which follows in <reference osisRef="Job.15.3">Job 15:3</reference>, as <hi type="italic">verb. fin.:</hi> <hi type="italic">se défend-il par des vaines paroles;</hi> but though the <hi type="italic">inf. abs.</hi> is so used in an historical clause (<reference osisRef="Job.15.35">Job 15:35</reference>), it is not an interrogative. Ewald takes it as the subject: “to reprove with words-avails not, and speeches - whereby one does no good;” but though דּבר and מלּים might be used without any further defining, as in λογομαχεῖν (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.14">2Ti 2:14</reference>) and λογομαχία (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.4">1Ti 6:4</reference>), the form of <reference osisRef="Job.15.3">Job 15:3</reference> is opposed to such an explanation. The <hi type="italic">inf. abs.</hi> is connected as a gerund (<hi type="italic">redarguendo s. disputando</hi>) with the verbs in the question, <reference osisRef="Job.15.2">Job 15:2</reference>; and the elliptical relative clause יסכּן לא is best, as referring to things, according to <reference osisRef="Job.35.3">Job 35:3</reference> : <hi type="italic">sermone</hi> (דּבד from דּבר, as <hi type="italic">sermo</hi> from <hi type="italic">serere</hi>) <hi type="italic">qui non prodest;</hi> בּם יועיל לא, on the other hand, to persons, <hi type="italic">verbis quibus nil utilitatis affert.</hi> Eliphaz does not censure Job for arguing, but for defending himself by such useless and purposeless utterances of his feeling. But still more than that: his speeches are not only unsatisfactory and unbecoming, אף, <hi type="italic">accedit quod</hi> (cumulative like <reference osisRef="Job.14.3">Job 14:3</reference>), they are moreover irreligious, since by doubting the justice of God they deprive religion of its fundamental assumption, and diminish the reverence due to God. יראה in such an objective sense as <reference osisRef="Ps.19.10">Psa 19:10</reference> almost corresponds to the idea of religion. שׂיחה לפני־אל is to be understood, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.102.1">Psa 102:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.142.3">Psa 142:3</reference> (comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.64.2">Psa 64:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.104.34">Psa 104:34</reference>): before God, and consequently customary devotional meditation, here of the disposition of mind indispensable to prayer, viz., devotion, and especially reverential awe, which Job depreciates (גּרע, <hi type="italic">detrahere</hi>). His speeches are mostly directed towards God; but they are violent and reproachful, therefore irreverent in form and substance.
entries.79bbdcb9c8e70c75cd9f8bda08cfb953eb732cd5: <reference osisRef="Job.15.7-Job.10.7">Job 15:7-10   7</reference>  Wast thou as the first one born as a man, <div eID="gen7463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7464" type="x-p"/> And hast thou been brought forth before the hills?   8  Hast thou attended to the counsel of Eloah, <div eID="gen7464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7465" type="x-p"/> And hast thou kept wisdom to thyself?   9  What dost thou know that we have not known? <div eID="gen7465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7466" type="x-p"/> Doest thou understand what we have not been acquainted with? 10  Both grey-haired and aged are among us, <div eID="gen7466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7467" type="x-p"/> Older in days than thy father. <div eID="gen7467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7468" type="x-p"/> The question in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.15.7">Job 15:7</reference></hi> assumes that the first created man, because coming direct from the hand of God, had the most direct and profoundest insight into the mysteries of the world which came into existence at the same time as himself. Schlottman calls to mind an ironical proverbial expression of the Hindus: “Yea, indeed, he is the first man; no wonder that he is so wise” (Roberts, <hi type="italic">Orient. Illustr.</hi> p. 276). It is not to be translated: wast thou born as the first man, which is as inadmissible as the translation of אחת מעט, Hag 2:6, by “a little” (vid., Köhler <hi type="italic">in loc</hi>.); rather ראישׁון (i.e., ראישׁון, as <reference osisRef="Josh.21.10">Jos 21:10</reference>, formed from ראשׁ, like the Arabic <hi type="italic">raı̂s</hi>, from <hi type="italic">ras</hi>, if it is not perhaps a mere incorrect amalgamation of the forms ראשׁון and רשׁון, <reference osisRef="Job.8.8">Job 8:8</reference>) is in apposition with the subject, and אדם is to be regarded as predicate, according to Ges. §139, 2. Raschi’s translation is also impossible: wast thou born before Adam? for this Greek form of expression, πρῶτος μον, Joh 1:15, Joh 1:30; Joh 15:18 (comp. <hi type="italic">Odyss</hi>. xi. 481f., σεῖο μακάρτατος), is strange to the Hebrew. In the parallel question, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.15.7">Job 15:7</reference></hi>, Umbr., Schlottm., and Renan (following Ewald) see a play upon Pro 8:24.: art thou the demiurgic Wisdom itself? But the introductory proverbs (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.9">Prov 1-9</reference>) are more recent than the book of Job (vid., <hi type="italic">supra</hi>, p. 24), and indeed probably, as we shall show elsewhere, belong to the time of Jehoshaphat. Consequently the more probable relation is that the writer of Pro 8:24. has adopted words from the book of Job in describing the pre-existence of the Chokma. Was Job, a higher spirit-nature, brought forth, i.e., as it were amidst the pangs of travail (חוללת, <hi type="italic">Pulal</hi> from חול, חיל), before the hills? for the angels, according to Scripture, were created before man, and even before the visible universe (vid., Job 38:4.). Hirz., Ew., Schlottm., and others erroneously translate the <hi type="italic">futt</hi>. in the questions, <reference osisRef="Job.15.8">Job 15:8</reference>, as <hi type="italic">praes</hi>. All the verbs in <reference osisRef="Job.15.7">Job 15:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.15.8">Job 15:8</reference>, are under the control of the retrospective character which is given to the verses by ראישׁון; comp. Job 10:10., where זכר־נא has the same influence, and also <reference osisRef="Job.3.3">Job 3:3</reference>, where the historical sense of אוּלד depends not upon the syntax, but upon logical necessity. Translate therefore: didst thou attend in the secret council (סוד, like <reference osisRef="Jer.23.18">Jer 23:18</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.89.8">Psa 89:8</reference>) of Eloah (according to the correct form of writing in Codd. and in Kimchi, <hi type="italic">Michlol </hi>54 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, הבסוד, like <reference osisRef="Job.15.11">Job 15:11</reference> המעט and <reference osisRef="Job.22.13">Job 22:13</reference> הבעד, with <hi type="italic">Beth raph.</hi> and without <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi>),<note placement="foot">As a rule, the interrogative He, when pointed with <hi type="italic">Pathach</hi>, has <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi> against the <hi type="italic">Pathach</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.5">2Sa 7:5</reference>; this, however, falls away (among other instances) when the syllable immediately following the <hi type="italic">He</hi> has the tone, as in the two examples given above (comp. also האל, <reference osisRef="Job.8.3">Job 8:3</reference>; הלאל, <reference osisRef="Job.13.7">Job 13:7</reference>), or the usual <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi> (<hi type="italic">Metheg</hi>) which stands in the <hi type="italic">antepenultima</hi> (Bär, <hi type="italic">Metheg-Setzung</hi>, §23</note> and didst then acquire for thyself (גרע, here <hi type="italic">attrahere</hi>, like the Arabic, <hi type="italic">sorbere</hi>, to suck in) wisdom? by which one is reminded of Prometheus’ fire stolen from heaven. Nay, Job can boast of no extraordinary wisdom. The friends - as Eliphaz, <reference osisRef="Job.15.9">Job 15:9</reference>, says in their name - are his contemporaries; and if he desires to appeal to the teaching of his father, and of his ancestors generally, let them know that there are hoary-headed men among themselves, whose discernment is deeper by reason of their more advanced age. גּם is inverted, like <reference osisRef="Job.2.10">Job 2:10</reference> (which see); and at the same time, since it is sued twice, it is correlative: <hi type="italic">etiam inter nos et cani et senes. </hi> Most modern expositors think that Eliphaz, “in modestly concealed language” (Ewald), refers to himself. But the reference would be obvious enough; and wherefore this modest concealing, which is so little suited to the character of Eliphaz? Moreover, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.15.10">Job 15:10</reference> </hi>does not sound as if speaking merely of one, and in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.15.10">Job 15:10</reference></hi> Eliphaz would make himself older than he appears to be, for it is nowhere implied that Job is a young man in comparison with him. We therefore with Umbreit explain בּנוּ: in our generation. Thus it sounds more like the Arabic, both in words (<hi type="italic">kebı̂r</hi> Arab., usual in the signif. <hi type="italic">grandaevus</hi>) and in substance. Eliphaz appeals to the source of reliable tradition, since they have even among their races and districts mature old men, and since, indeed, according to Job’s own admission (<reference osisRef="Job.12.12">Job 12:12</reference>), there is “wisdom among the ancient ones.”
entries.f8c80d83cebfa27f98a92b7b78c046a3ebbcd5d4: <reference osisRef="Job.15.11-Job.13.11">Job 15:11-13 11</reference>  Are the consolations of God too small for thee, <div eID="gen7468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7469" type="x-p"/> And a word thus tenderly spoken with thee? 12  What overpowers thy hearts? <div eID="gen7469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7470" type="x-p"/> And why do thine eyes wink, 13  That thou turnest thy snorting against God, <div eID="gen7470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7471" type="x-p"/> And sendest forth such words from thy mouth? <div eID="gen7471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7472" type="x-p"/> By the consolations of God, Eliphaz means the promises in accordance with the majesty and will of God, by which he and the other friends have sought to cheer him, of course presupposing a humble resignation to the just hand of God. By “a word (spoken) in gentleness to him,” he means the gentle tone which they have maintained, while he has passionately opposed them. לאט, elsewhere לאט (e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.8.6">Isa 8:6</reference>, of the softly murmuring and gently flowing Siloah), from אט (declined, אטּי), with the neutral, adverbial ל (as לבטה), signifies: with a soft step, gently, The word has no connection with לוּט, לאט, to cover over, and is not third <hi type="italic">praet</hi>. (as it is regarded by Raschi, after Chajug): which he has gently said to you, or that which has gently befallen you; in which, as in Fürst’s <hi type="italic">Handwörterbuch</hi>, the notions <hi type="italic">secrete</hi> (Jdg 4:21, Targ. בּרז, in secret) and <hi type="italic">leniter</hi> are referred to one root. Are these divine consolations, and these so gentle addresses, too small for thee (מעט ממך, <hi type="italic">opp</hi>. 1Ki 19:7), i.e., beneath thy dignity, and unworthy of they notice? What takes away (לקה, <hi type="italic">auferre, abripere,</hi> as frequently) thy heart (here of wounded pride), and why do thine eyes gleam, that thou turnest (השׁיב, not <hi type="italic">revertere</hi>, but <hi type="italic">vertere</hi>, as freq.) thy ill-humour towards God, and utterest מלּין (so here, not מלּים) words, which, because they are without meaning and intelligence, are nothing but words? רזם, ἅπ. γεγρ., is transposed from רמז, to wink, i.e., to make known by gestures and grimaces, - a word which does not occur in biblical, but is very common in post-biblical, Hebrew (e.g., חרשׁ רומז ונרמז, a deaf and dumb person expresses himself and is answered by a language of signs). Modern expositors arbitrarily understand a rolling of the eyes; it is more natural to think of the vibration of the eye-lashes or eye-brows. רוּח, <reference osisRef="Job.15.13">Job 15:13</reference>, is as in Jdg 8:3; <reference osisRef="Isa.25.4">Isa 25:4</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.13.11">Job 13:11</reference>, and freq. used of passionate excitement, which is thus expressed because it manifests itself in πνέειν (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.1">Act 9:1</reference>), and has its rise in the πνεῦμα (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.9">Ecc 7:9</reference>). Job ought to control this angry spirit, θυμός (<hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 198); but he allows it to burst forth, and makes even God the object on which he vents his anger in impetuous language. How much better it would be for him, if he would search within himself (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.39">Lam 3:39</reference>) for the reason of those sufferings which so deprive him of his self-control!
entries.8c90033f71236a3ffca3222bf3a6a3516e5d7270: <reference osisRef="Job.15.14-Job.16.14">Job 15:14-16 14</reference>  What is mortal man that he should be pure, <div eID="gen7472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7473" type="x-p"/> And that he who is born of woman should be righteous? 15  He trusteth not His holy ones, <div eID="gen7473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7474" type="x-p"/> And the heavens are not pure in His eyes: 16  How much less the abominable and corrupt, <div eID="gen7474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7475" type="x-p"/> Man, who drinketh iniquity as water! <div eID="gen7475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7476" type="x-p"/> The exclamation in <reference osisRef="Job.15.14">Job 15:14</reference> is like the utterance: mortal man and man born flesh of flesh cannot be entirely sinless. Even “the holy ones” and “the heavens” are not. The former are, as in <reference osisRef="Job.5.1">Job 5:1</reference>, according to <reference osisRef="Job.4.18">Job 4:18</reference>, the angels as beings of light (whether קדשׁ signifies to be light from the very first, spotlessly pure, or, vid., <hi type="italic">Psalter</hi>, i. 588f., to be separated, distinct, and hence exalted above what is common); the latter is not another expression for the אנגּלי מרומא (Targ.), the “angels of the heights,” but שׁמים is the word used for the highest spheres in which they dwell (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.25.5">Job 25:5</reference>); for the angels are certainly not corporeal, but, like all created things, in space, and the Scriptures everywhere speak of angels and the starry heavens together. Hence the angels are called the morning stars in <reference osisRef="Job.38.7">Job 38:7</reference>, and hence both stars and angels are called צבא השׁמים and צבאות (vid., <hi type="italic">Genesis</hi>. S. 128). Even the angels and the heavens are finite, and consequently are not of a nature absolutely raised above the possibility of sin and contamination. <div eID="gen7476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7477" type="x-p"/> Eliphaz repeats here what he has already said, Job 4:18.; but he does it intentionally, since he wishes still more terribly to describe human uncleanness to Job (Oetinger). In that passage אף was merely the sign of an anti-climax, here כּי אף is <hi type="italic">quanto minus.</hi> Eliphaz refers to the hereditary infirmity and sin of human nature in <reference osisRef="Job.15.14">Job 15:14</reference>, here (<reference osisRef="Job.15.16">Job 15:16</reference>) to man’s own free choice of that which works his destruction. He uses the strongest imaginable words to describe one <hi type="italic">actualiter</hi> and <hi type="italic">originaliter</hi> corrupted. נתעב denotes one who is become an abomination, or the abominated = abominable (Ges. §134, 1); נאלח, one thoroughly corrupted (Arabic <hi type="italic">alacha</hi>, in the medial VIII conjugation: to become sour, which reminds one of ζύμη, Rabb. שׂאר שׁבּעסּה, as an image of evil, and especially of evil desire). It is further said of him (an expression which Elihu adopts, <reference osisRef="Job.34.7">Job 34:7</reference>), that he drinks up evil like water. The figure is like <reference osisRef="Prov.26.6">Pro 26:6</reference>, comp. on <reference osisRef="Ps.73.10">Psa 73:10</reference>, and implies that he lusts after sin, and that it is become a necessity of his nature, and is to his nature what water is to the thirsty. Even Job does not deny this corruption of man (<reference osisRef="Job.14.4">Job 14:4</reference>), but the inferences which the friends draw in reference to him he cannot acknowledge. The continuation of Eliphaz' speech shows how they render this acknowledgment impossible to him.
entries.a5e5d571f83dad9f314537c507ecef6b702769f8: Job 15:17-19 17  I will inform thee, hear me! <div eID="gen7477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7478" type="x-p"/> And what I have myself seen that I will declare, 18  Things which wise men declare <div eID="gen7478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7479" type="x-p"/> Without concealment from their fathers - 19  To them alone was the land given over, <div eID="gen7479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7480" type="x-p"/> And no stranger had passed in their midst - : <div eID="gen7480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7481" type="x-p"/> Eliphaz, as in his first speech, introduces the dogma with which he confronts Job with a solemn preface: in the former case it had its rise in a revelation, here it is supported by his own experience and reliable tradition; for חזיתי is not intended as meaning ecstatic vision (Schlottm.). The poet uses חזה also of sensuous vision, <reference osisRef="Job.8.17">Job 8:17</reference>; and of observation and knowledge by means of the senses, not only the more exalted, as Job 19:26., but of any kind (<reference osisRef="Job.23.9">Job 23:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.24.1">Job 24:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.27.12">Job 27:12</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.36.25">Job 36:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.34.32">Job 34:32</reference>), in the widest sense. זה is used as neuter, <reference osisRef="Gen.6.15">Gen 6:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.13.8">Exo 13:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.30.13">Exo 30:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.11.4">Lev 11:4</reference>, and freq.<note placement="foot">So also <reference osisRef="Ps.56.10">Psa 56:10</reference>, where I now prefer to translate “This I know,” זה neuter, like <reference osisRef="Prov.24.12">Pro 24:12</reference>, and referring forward as above, Job 15:17.</note> (comp. the neuter הוּא, <reference osisRef="Job.13.16">Job 13:16</reference>, and often), and זה־חזיתי is a relative clause (Ges. §122, 2): <hi type="italic">quod conspexi,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Job.19.19">Job 19:19</reference> <hi type="italic">quos amo,</hi> and <reference osisRef="Ps.74.2">Psa 74:2</reference> <hi type="italic">in quo habitas,</hi> comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.104.8">Psa 104:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.26">Psa 104:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.23.22">Pro 23:22</reference>, where the punctuation throughout proceeds from the correct knowledge of the syntax. The <hi type="italic">waw</hi> of ואספרה is the <hi type="italic">waw apodosis,</hi> which is customary (Nägelsbach, §111, 1, <hi type="italic">b</hi>) after relative clauses (e.g., Num 23:3), or what is the same thing, participles (e.g., <reference osisRef="Prov.23.24">Pro 23:24</reference>): <hi type="italic">et narrabo</hi> = <hi type="italic">ea narrabo</hi>. In <reference osisRef="Job.15.18">Job 15:18</reference> ולא כחדו is, logically at least, subordinate to יגידו, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.3.9">Isa 3:9</reference>,<note placement="foot">Heidenheim refers to Hos 8:2 for the position of the words, but there <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> may also be an apposition: we know thee, we Israel.</note> as the Targum of the Antwerp Polyglott well translates: “what wise men declare, without concealing (ולא מכדבין), from the tradition of their fathers;” whereas all the other old translations, including Luther’s, have missed the right meaning. These fathers to whom this doctrine respecting the fate of evil-doers is referred, lived, as Eliphaz says in <reference osisRef="Job.15.19">Job 15:19</reference>, in the land of their birth, and did not mingle themselves with strangers, consequently their manner of viewing things, and their opinions, have in their favour the advantage of independence, of being derived from their own experience, and also of a healthy development undisturbed by any foreign influences, and their teaching may be accounted pure and unalloyed. <div eID="gen7481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7482" type="x-p"/> Eliphaz thus indirectly says, that the present is not free from such influences, and Ewald is consequently of opinion that the individuality of the Israelitish poet peeps out here, and a state of things is indicated like that which came about after the fall of Samaria in the reign of Manasseh. Hirzel also infers from Eliphaz' words, that at the time when the book was written the poet’s fatherland was desecrated by some foreign rule, and considers it an indication for determining the time at which the book was composed. But how groundless and deceptive this is! The way in which Eliphaz commends ancient traditional lore is so genuinely Arabian, that there is but the faintest semblance of a reason for supposing the poet to have thrown his own history and national peculiarity so vividly into the working up of the <hi type="italic">rôle</hi> of another. Purity of race was, from the earliest times, considered by “the sons of the East” as a sign of highest nobility, and hence Eliphaz traces back his teaching to a time when his race could boast of the greatest freedom from intermixture with any other. Schlottmann prefers to interpret <reference osisRef="Job.15.19">Job 15:19</reference> as referring to the “nobler primeval races of man” (without, however, referring to <reference osisRef="Job.8.8">Job 8:8</reference>), but הארץ does not signify the earth here, but: country, as in <reference osisRef="Job.30.8">Job 30:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.22.8">Job 22:8</reference>, and elsewhere, and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.15.19">Job 15:19</reference></hi> seems to refer to nations: זר = <hi type="italic">barbarus</hi> (perhaps Semitic: בּרבּר, ὁ ἔξω). Nevertheless it is unnecessary to suppose that Eliphaz' time was one of foreign domination, as the Assyrian-Chaldean time was for Israel: it is sufficient to imagine it as a time when the tribes of the desert were becoming intermixed, from migration, commerce, and feud. <div eID="gen7482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7483" type="x-p"/> Now follows the doctrine of the wise men, which springs from a venerable primitive age, an age as yet undisturbed by any strange way of thinking (modern enlightenment and free thinking, as we should say), and is supported by Eliphaz' own experience. (Note: Communication from Consul Wetzstein: If this verse affirms that the freer a people is from intermixture with other races, the purer is its tradition, it gives expression to a principle derived from experience, which needs no proof. Even European races, especially the Scandinavians, furnish proof of this in their customs, language, and traditions, although in this case certain elements of their indigenous character have vanished with the introduction of Christianity. A more complete parallel is furnished by the wandering tribes of the '<hi type="italic">Aneze</hi> and <hi type="italic">Sharârât</hi> of the Syrian deserts, people who have indeed had their struggles, and have even been weakened by emigration, but have certainly never lost their political and religious autonomy, and have preserved valuable traditions which may be traced to the earliest antiquity. It is unnecessary to prove this by special instance, when the whole outer and inner life of these peoples can be regarded as the best commentary on the biblical accounts of the patriarchal age. It is, however, not so much the <hi type="italic">fact</hi> that the evil-doer receives his punishment, in favour of which Eliphaz appeals to the teaching handed down from the fathers, as rather the <hi type="italic">belief in it</hi>, consequently in a certain degree the dogma of a moral order in the world. This dogma is an essential element of the ancient Abrahamic religion of the desert tribes - that primitive religion which formed the basis of the Mosaic, and side by side with it was continued among the nomads of the desert; which, shortly before the appearance of Christianity in the country east of Jordan, gave birth to mild doctrines, doctrines which tended to prepare the way for the teaching of the gospel; which at that very time, according to historical testimony, also prevailed in the towns of the <hi type="italic">Higâz</hi>, and was first displaced again by the Jemanic idolatry, and limited to the desert, in the second century after Christ, during the repeated migrations of the southern Arabs; which gave the most powerful impulse to the rise of Islam, and furnished its best elements; which, towards the end of the last century, brought about the reform of Islamism in the province of <hi type="italic">Negd</hi>, and produced the <hi type="italic">Wahabee</hi> doctrine; and which, finally, is continued even to the present day by the name of <hi type="italic">Dîn Ibrâhîm</hi>, “Religion of Abraham,” as a faithful tradition of the fathers, among the vast Ishmaelitish tribes of the Syrian desert, “to whom alone the land is given over, and into whose midst no stranger has penetrated.” Had this <hi type="italic">cultus</hi> spread among settled races with a higher education, it might have been taught also in writings: if, however, portions of writings in reference to it, which have been handed down to us by the Arabic, are to be regarded as unauthentic, it may also in '<hi type="italic">Irâk</hi> have been mixed with the Sabian <hi type="italic">worship</hi> of the stars; but among the nomads it will have always been only oral, taught by the poets in song, and contained in the fine traditions handed down uncorrupted from father to son, and practised in life. <div eID="gen7483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7484" type="x-p"/> It is a dogma of this religion (of which I shall speak more fully in the introduction to my <hi type="italic">Anthologie von Poesien der Wanderstâmme</hi>), that the pious will be rewarded by God in his life and in his descendants, the wicked punished in his life and in his descendants; and it may also, in <reference osisRef="Job.15.19">Job 15:19</reference>, be indirectly said that the land of Eliphaz has preserved this faith, in accordance with tradition, purer than Job’s land. If Eliphaz was from the Petraean town of <hi type="italic">Têmân</hi> (which we merely suggest as possible here), he might indeed rightly assert that no strange race had become naturalized there; for that hot, sterile land, poorly supplied with water, had nothing inviting to the emigrant or marauder, and its natives remain there only by virtue of the proverb: <hi type="italic">lôlâ hhibb el - wattan quat . tâl , lakân dâr eṡsû' charâb</hi>, “Did not the love of one’s country slay (him who is separated from it), the barren country would be uninhabited.” Job certainly could not affirm the same of his native country, if this is, with the Syrian tradition, to be regarded as the <hi type="italic">Nukra</hi> (on this point, vid., the Appendix). As the richest province of Syria, it has, from the earliest time to the present, always been an apple of contention, and has not only frequently changed its rulers, but even its inhabitants.)
entries.30c1e26203f409d8de5a7883fbb17f9a9bf91262: Job 15:20-24 20  So long as the ungodly liveth he suffereth, <div eID="gen7484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7485" type="x-p"/> And numbered years are reserved for the tyrant. 21  Terrors sound in his ears; <div eID="gen7485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7486" type="x-p"/> In time of peace the destroyer cometh upon him. 22  He believeth not in a return from darkness, <div eID="gen7486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7487" type="x-p"/> And he is selected for the sword. 23  He roameth about after bread: “Ah! where is it?” <div eID="gen7487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7488" type="x-p"/> He knoweth that a dark day is near at hand for him. 24  Trouble and anguish terrify him; <div eID="gen7488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7489" type="x-p"/> They seize him as a king ready to the battle. <div eID="gen7489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7490" type="x-p"/> All the days of the ungodly he (the ungodly) is sensible of pain. רשׁע stands, like <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> in <reference osisRef="Gen.9.6">Gen 9:6</reference>, by the closer definition; here however so, that this defining ends after the manner of a premiss, and is begun by הוּא after the manner of a conclusion. מתחולל, he writhes, i.e., suffers inward anxiety and distress in the midst of all outward appearance of happiness. Most expositors translate the next line: and throughout the number of the years, which are reserved to the tyrant. But (1) this parallel definition of time appended by <hi type="italic">waw</hi> makes the sense drawling; (2) the change of עריץ (oppressor, tyrant) for רשׁע leads one to expect a fresh affirmation, hence it is translated by the lxx: ἔτη δὲ ἀριθμητὰ δεδομένα δυνάστῃ. The predicate is, then, like <reference osisRef="Job.32.7">Job 32:7</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.29.10">Job 29:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.2.4">Job 2:4</reference> (Ges. §148), <hi type="italic">per</hi> <hi type="italic">attractionem</hi> in the <hi type="italic">plur</hi>. instead of in the sing., and especially with מספּר followed by <hi type="italic">gen. plur.;</hi> this attraction is adopted by our author, <reference osisRef="Job.21.21">Job 21:21</reference>; Job 38:21. The meaning is not, that numbered, i.e., few, years are secretly appointed to the tyrant, which must have been <hi type="italic">sh'nôth mispâr ,</hi> a reversed position of the words, as <reference osisRef="Job.16.22">Job 16:22</reference>; Num 9:20 (vid., Gesenius’ <hi type="italic">Thes.</hi>); but a (limited, appointed) number of years is reserved to the tyrant (צפן as <reference osisRef="Job.24.1">Job 24:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.19">Job 21:19</reference>, comp. טמן, <reference osisRef="Job.20.26">Job 20:26</reference>; Mercerus: <hi type="italic">occulto decreto definiti</hi>), after the expiration of which his punishment begins. The thought expressed by the Targ., Syr., and Jerome would be suitable: and the number of the years (that he has to live unpunished) is hidden from the tyrant; but if this were the poet’s meaning, he would have written שׁניו, and must have written מן־העריץ. <div eID="gen7490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7491" type="x-p"/> With regard to the following <reference osisRef="Job.15.21-Job.15.24">Job 15:21-24</reference>, it is doubtful whether only the evil-doer’s anxiety of spirit is described in amplification of הוא מתחולל, or also how the terrible images from which he suffers in his conscience are realized, and how he at length helplessly succumbs to the destruction which his imagination had long foreboded. A satisfactory and decisive answer to this question is hardly possible; but considering that the real crisis is brought on by Eliphaz later, and fully described, it seems more probable that what has an objective tone in <reference osisRef="Job.15.21-Job.15.24">Job 15:21-24</reference> is controlled by what has been affirmed respecting the evil conscience of the ungodly, and is to be understood accordingly. The sound of terrible things (startling dangers) rings in his ears; the devastator comes upon him (בוא <hi type="italic">seq. acc.</hi> as <reference osisRef="Job.20.22">Job 20:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.28.22">Pro 28:22</reference>; comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.28.15">Isa 28:15</reference>) in the midst of his prosperity. He anticipates it ere it happens. From the darkness by which he feels himself menaced, he believes not (האמין <hi type="italic">seq. infin.</hi> as <reference osisRef="Ps.27.13">Psa 27:13</reference>, לראות, of confident hope) to return; i.e., overwhelmed with a consciousness of his guilt, he cannot, in the presence of this darkness which threatens him, raise to the hope of rescue from it, and he is really - as his consciousness tells him - צפוּ (like עשׂוּ, <reference osisRef="Job.41.25">Job 41:25</reference>; Ges. §75, rem. 5; <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> צפוי, which is omitted in our printed copies, contrary to the testimony of the Masora and the authority of correct MSS), spied out for, appointed to the sword, i.e., of God (<reference osisRef="Job.19.29">Job 19:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.31.8">Isa 31:8</reference>), or decreed by God. In the midst of abundance he is harassed by the thought of becoming poor; he wanders about in search of bread, anxiously looking out and asking where? (abrupt, like הנה, <reference osisRef="Job.9.19">Job 9:19</reference>), i.e., where is any to be found, whence can I obtain it? The lxx translates contrary to the connection, and with a strange misunderstanding of the passage: κατατέτακται δὲ δἰς σῖτα γυψίν (איּה לחם, food for the vulture). He sees himself in the mirror of the future thus reduced to beggary; he knows that a day of darkness stands in readiness (נכון, like <reference osisRef="Job.18.12">Job 18:12</reference>), is at his hand, i.e., close upon him (בּידו, elsewhere in this sense ליד, <reference osisRef="Ps.140.6">Psa 140:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.3">1Sa 19:3</reference>, and על־ידי, <reference osisRef="Job.1.14">Job 1:14</reference>). <div eID="gen7491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7492" type="x-p"/> In accordance with the previous exposition, we shall now interpret וּמצוּקה צר, <reference osisRef="Job.15.24">Job 15:24</reference>, not of need and distress, but subjectively of fear and oppression. They come upon him suddenly and irresistibly; it seizes or overpowers him (תּתקפהוּ with neutral subject; an unknown something, a dismal power) as a king עתיד לכּידור. lxx ὥσπερ στρατηγὸς πρωτοστάτης πίπτων, like a leader falling in the first line of the battle, which is an imaginary interpretation of the text. The translation of the Targum also, <hi type="italic">sicut regem qui paratus est ad scabellum</hi> (to serve the conqueror as a footstool), furnishes no explanation. Another Targum translation (in Nachmani and elsewhere) is: <hi type="italic">sicut rex qui paratus est circumdare se legionibus</hi>. According to this, כידור comes from כּדר, to surround, be round (comp. כּתר, whence כּתר, Assyr. <hi type="italic">cudar</hi>, κίδαρις, perhaps also הזר, Syr. חדר, whence <hi type="italic">chedor</hi>, a circle, round about); and it is assumed, that as כּדּוּר signifies a ball (not only in Talmudic, but also in <reference osisRef="Isa.22.18">Isa 22:18</reference>, which is to be translated: rolling he rolleth thee into a ball, a ball in a spacious land), so כּידור, a round encampment, an army encamped in a circle, synon. of מעגּל. In the first signification the word certainly furnishes no suitable sense in connection with עתיד; but one may, with Kimchi, suppose that כידור, like the Italian <hi type="italic">torniamento</hi>, denotes the circle as well as the tournament, or the round of conflict, i.e., the conflict which moves round about, like tumult of battle, which last is a suitable meaning here. The same appropriate meaning is attained, however, if the root is taken, like the Arabic <hi type="italic">kdr</hi>, in the signification <hi type="italic">turbidum esse</hi> (comp. קדר, <reference osisRef="Job.6.16">Job 6:16</reference>), which is adopted of misfortunes as troubled experiences of life (according to which Schultens translates: <hi type="italic">destinatus est ad turbulentissimas fortunas,</hi> beginning a new thought with עתיד, which is not possible, since כמלך by itself is no complete figure), and may perhaps also be referred to the tumult of battle, <hi type="italic">tumultus bellici conturbatio</hi> (Rosenm.); or of, with Fleischer, one starts from another turn of the idea of the root, viz., to be compressed, solid, thick, which is a more certain way gives the meaning of a dense crowd.<note placement="foot">The Arab. verb <hi type="italic">kdr</hi> belongs to the root <hi type="italic">kd</hi>, to smite, thrust, <hi type="italic">quatere, percutere, tundere, trudere;</hi> a root that has many branches. It is I. transitive <hi type="italic">cadara</hi> (fut. <hi type="italic">jacduru</hi>, inf. <hi type="italic">cadr</hi>) - by the non-adoption of which from the original lexicons our lexicographers have deprived the whole etymological development of its groundwork - in the signification to <hi type="italic">pour, hurl down, pour out,</hi> e.g., <hi type="italic">cadara-l-mâa,</hi> he has spilt, poured out, thrown down the water; hence in the medial VII. form incadara intransitive, to fall, fall down, chiefly of water and other fluids, as of the rain which pours down from heaven, of a cascade, and the like; then improperly of a bird of prey which shoots down from the air upon its prey (e.g., in the poetry in Beidhâwi on <hi type="italic">Sur</hi>. 81, 2: “The hawk saw some bustards on the plain <hi type="italic">f'ancadara</hi>, and rushed down”); of a hostile host which rushes upon the enemy first possible signification for כידור]; of a man, horse, etc., which runs very swiftly, <hi type="italic">effuse currit, effuso curru ruit;</hi> of the stars that shall fall from heaven at the last day (Sur. 81, 2). Then also II. intransitive <hi type="italic">cadara</hi> (fut. <hi type="italic">jacdiru</hi>) with the secondary form <hi type="italic">cadira</hi> (fut. <hi type="italic">jacdaru</hi>) and <hi type="italic">cadura</hi> (fut. <hi type="italic">jacduru</hi>), prop. to be shaken and jolted; then also of fluid things, mixed and mingled, made turgid, unclean, i.e., by shaking, jolting, stirring, etc., with the dregs (the <hi type="italic">cudâre</hi> or <hi type="italic">cudâde</hi>); then gen. <hi type="italic">turbidum</hi>, <hi type="italic">non limpidum</hi> (<hi type="italic">opp</hi>. Arab. <hi type="italic">ṣf'</hi>), with a similar transition of meaning to that in <hi type="italic">turbare</hi> (comp. <hi type="italic">deturbare</hi>) and the German <hi type="italic">trüben</hi> (comp. <hi type="italic">traben</hi> or <hi type="italic">trappen</hi>, <hi type="italic">treiben</hi>, <hi type="italic">treffen</hi>). The primary meaning of the root takes another III. turn in the derived adjectives <hi type="italic">cudur</hi>, <hi type="italic">cudurr</hi>, <hi type="italic">cundur</hi>, <hi type="italic">cunâdir</hi>, <hi type="italic">compressed</hi>, <hi type="italic">solid</hi>, <hi type="italic">thick</hi>; the last word with us (Germans) forms a transition from <hi type="italic">cadir</hi>, <hi type="italic">cadr</hi>, <hi type="italic">cadîr</hi>, dull, slimy, yeasty, etc., inasmuch as we speak of <hi type="italic">dickes Bier</hi> (thick beer), etc., <hi type="italic">cerevisia spissa</hi>, <hi type="italic">de la bière épaisse</hi>. Here the point of contact of the word כידור, tumult of battle, κλόνος ἀνδρῶν, seems indicated: a dense crowd and tumult, where one is close upon another; as also נלחם, מלחמה, signify not reciprocal destruction, slaughter, but to press firmly and closely upon one another, a dense crowd. - Fl.</note> <div eID="gen7492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7493" type="x-p"/> Since, therefore, a suitable meaning is obtained in two ways, the natural conjecture, which is commended by <reference osisRef="Prov.6.11">Pro 6:11</reference>, עתיד לכּידון, <hi type="italic">paratus ad hastam </hi>= <hi type="italic">peritus hastae</hi> (Hupf.), according to <reference osisRef="Job.3.8">Job 3:8</reference>) where ערר = לערר), may be abandoned. The signification <hi type="italic">circuitus</hi> has the most support, according to which Saadia and Parchon also explain, and we have preferred to translate round of battle rather than tumult of conflict; Jerome’s translation, <hi type="italic">qui praeparatur ad praelium,</hi> seems also to be gained in the same manner.
entries.5d24323015e3fb806d25892bdea35bf61f63cf0c: Job 15:25-30 25  Because he stretched out his hand against God, <div eID="gen7493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7494" type="x-p"/> And was insolent towards the Almighty; 26  He assailed Him with a stiff neck, <div eID="gen7494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7495" type="x-p"/> With the thick bosses of his shield; 27  Because he covered his face with his fatness, <div eID="gen7495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7496" type="x-p"/> And addeth fat to his loins, 28  And inhabited desolated cities, <div eID="gen7496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7497" type="x-p"/> Houses which should not be inhabited, <div eID="gen7497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7498" type="x-p"/> Which were appointed to be ruins. 29  He shall not be rich, and his substance shall not continue <div eID="gen7498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7499" type="x-p"/> And their substance boweth not to the ground. 30  He escapeth not darkness; <div eID="gen7499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7500" type="x-p"/> The flame withereth his shoots; <div eID="gen7500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7501" type="x-p"/> And he perisheth in the breath of His mouth. <div eID="gen7501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7502" type="x-p"/> This strophe has periodic members: <reference osisRef="Job.15.25-Job.15.28">Job 15:25-28</reference> an antecedent clause with a double beginning (כּי־נטה because he has stretched out, כּי־כסּה because he has covered; whereas ירוּץ may be taken as more independent, but under the government of the כי that stands at the commencement of the sentence); <reference osisRef="Job.15.29">Job 15:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.15.30">Job 15:30</reference>, is the conclusion. Two chief sins are mentioned as the cause of the final destiny that comes upon the evil-doer: (1) his arrogant opposition to God, and (2) his contentment on the ruins of another’s prosperity. The first of these sins is described <reference osisRef="Job.15.25">Job 15:25</reference>-27. The <hi type="italic">fut.</hi> <hi type="italic">consec.</hi> is once used instead of the <hi type="italic">perf.,</hi> and the simple <hi type="italic">fut.</hi> is twice used with the signification of an <hi type="italic">imperf.</hi> (as <reference osisRef="Job.4.3">Job 4:3</reference> and freq.). The <hi type="italic">Hithpa.</hi> התגּבּר signifies here to maintain a heroic bearing, to play the hero; התעשּׁר to make one’s self rich, to play the part of a rich man, Pro 13:7. And בּצוּאר expresses the special prominence of the neck in his assailing God אל רוּץ, as <reference osisRef="Dan.8.6">Dan 8:6</reference>, comp. על, <reference osisRef="Job.16.14">Job 16:14</reference>); it is equivalent to <hi type="italic">erecto collo</hi> (Vulg.), and in meaning equivalent to ὕβρει (lxx). Also in <reference osisRef="Ps.75.6">Psa 75:6</reference>, בצואר (with <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, which there represents a distinctive)<note placement="foot">Vid., Dachselt’s <hi type="italic">Biblia Accentuata</hi>, p. 816.)</note> is absolute, in the sense of stiff-necked or hard-headed; for the parallels, as <reference osisRef="Ps.31.19">Psa 31:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.94.4">Psa 94:4</reference>, and especially the primary passage, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.3">1Sa 2:3</reference>, show that עתק is to be taken as an accusative of the object. The proud defiance with which he challengingly assails God, and renders himself insensible to the dispensations of God, which might bring him to a right way of thinking, is symbolized by the additional clause: with the thickness (עבי cognate form to עבי) of the bosses of his shields. גּב is the back (Arab. <hi type="italic">dhr</hi>) or boss (<hi type="italic">umbo</hi>) of the shield; the plurality of shields has reference to the diversified means by which he hardens himself. <reference osisRef="Job.15.27">Job 15:27</reference>, similarly to <reference osisRef="Ps.73.4-Ps.73.7">Psa 73:4-7</reference>, pictures this impregnable carnal security against all unrest and pain, to which, on account of his own sinfulness and the distress of others, the nobler-minded man is so sensitive: he has covered his face with his fat, so that by the accumulation of fat, for which he anxiously labours, it becomes a gross material lump of flesh, devoid of mind and soul, and made fat, i.e., added fat, caused it to accumulate, upon his loins (כּסל for כּסליו); עשׂה (which has nothing to do with Arab. <hi type="italic">gšâ</hi>, to cover) is used as in <reference osisRef="Job.14.9">Job 14:9</reference>, and in the phrase <hi type="italic">corpus facere</hi> (in Justin), in the sense of producing outwardly something from within. פּימה reminds one of πιμ-ελή (as Aquila and Symmachus translate here), <hi type="italic">o-pim-us,</hi> and of the Sanscrit <hi type="italic">piai ,</hi> to be fat (whence adj. <hi type="italic">pı̂van , pı̂vara ,</hi> πιαρός, part. <hi type="italic">pı̂na ,</hi> subst. according to Roth <hi type="italic">pı̂vas</hi>); the Arabic renders it probable that it is a contraction of פּאימה (Olsh. §171, <hi type="italic">b</hi>). The Jewish expositors explain it according to the misunderstood פּים,   <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.21">1Sa 13:21</reference>, of the furrows or wrinkles which are formed in flabby flesh, as if the <hi type="italic">ah</hi> were paragogic. <div eID="gen7502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7503" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Job.15.28">Job 15:28</reference> describes the second capital sin of the evil-doer. The desolated cities that he dwells in are not cities that he himself has laid waste; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.15.28">Job 15:28</reference></hi> distinctly refers to a divinely appointed punishment, for התעתּדוּ does not signify: which they (evil-doers) have made ruins (Hahn), which is neither probable from the change of number, nor accords with the meaning of the verb, which signifies “to appoint to something in the future.” Hirzel, by referring to the law, <reference osisRef="Deut.13.13-Deut.13.18">Deu 13:13-18</reference> (comp. 1Ki 16:34), which forbids the rebuilding of such cities as are laid under the curse, explains it to a certain extent more correctly. But such a play upon the requirements of the Mosaic law is in itself not probable in the book of Job, and here, as Löwenthal rightly remarks, is the less indicated, since it is not the dwelling in such cities that is forbidden, but only the rebuilding of them, so far as they had been destroyed; here, however, the reference is only to dwelling, not to rebuilding. The expression must therefore be understood more generally thus, that the powerful man settles down carelessly and indolently, without any fear of the judgments of God or respect for the manifestations of His judicial authority, in places in which the marks of a just divine retribution are still visible, and which are appointed to be perpetual monuments of the execution of divine judgments.<note placement="foot">For the elucidation of this interpretation of the passage, Consul Wetzstein has contributed the following: “As one who yields to inordinate passion is without sympathy cast from human society because he is called <hi type="italic">muqâtal rabbuh</hi>, 'one who is beaten in the conflict against his God' (since he has sinned against the holy command of chastity), and as no one ventures to pronounce the name of Satan because God has cursed him (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.14">Gen 3:14</reference>), without adding <hi type="italic">'alêh el-la'ne</hi>, 'God’s curse upon him!' so a man may not presume to inhabit places which God has appointed to desolation. Such villages and cities, which, according to tradition, have perished and been frequently overthrown (<hi type="italic">maqlûbe, muqêlîbe, munqualibe</hi>) by the visitation of divine judgment, are not uncommon on the borders of the desert. They are places, it is said, where the primary commandments of the religion of Abraham (<hi type="italic">Dîn Ibrâhim</hi>) have been impiously transgressed. Thus the city of <hi type="italic">Babylon</hi> will never be colonized by a Semitic tribe, because they hold the belief that it has been destroyed on account of Nimrod’s apostasy from God, and his hostility to His favoured one, <hi type="italic">Abraham</hi>. The tradition which has even been transferred by the tribes of Arabia Petraea into Islamism of the desolation of the city of <hi type="italic">Higr</hi> (or <hi type="italic">Medâin Sâlih</hi>) on account of disobedience to God, prevents any one from dwelling in that remarkable city, which consists of thousands of dwellings cut in the rock, some of which are richly ornamented; without looking round, and muttering prayers, the desert ranger hurries through, even as does the great procession of pilgrims to <hi type="italic">Mekka</hi>, from fear of incurring the punishment of God by the slightest delay in the accursed city. The destruction of <hi type="italic">Sodom</hi>, brought about by the violation of the right of hospitality (<reference osisRef="Gen.19.5">Gen 19:5</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.31.32">Job 31:32</reference>), is to be mentioned here, for this legend certainly belongs originally to the <hi type="italic">'Din Ibrâhîm'</hi> rather than to the Mosaic. At the source of the <hi type="italic">Rakkâd</hi> (the largest river of the Golan region) there are a number of erect and remarkably perforated jasper formations, which are called 'the bridal procession' (<hi type="italic">el-fârida</hi>). This bridal procession was turned to stone, because a woman of the party cleaned her child that had made itself dirty with a bread-cake (<hi type="italic">qurss</hi>). Near it is its village (<hi type="italic">Ufûne</hi>), which in spite of repeated attempts is no more to be inhabited. It remains forsaken, as an eternal witness that ingratitude (<hi type="italic">kufrân en-ni'ma</hi>), especially towards God, does not remain unpunished.</note> <div eID="gen7503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7504" type="x-p"/> Only by this rendering is the form of expression of the elliptical clause לא־ישׁבוּ למו explained. Hirz. refers למו to בּתּים: in which they do not dwell; but ל ישׁב does not signify: to dwell in a place, but: to settle down in a place; Schlottm. refers למו to the inhabitants: therein they dwell not themselves, i.e., where no one dwelt; but the אשׁר which would be required in this case as <hi type="italic">acc. localis </hi>could not be omitted. One might more readily, with Hahn, explain: those to whom they belong do not inhabit them; but it is linguistically impossible for למו to stand alone as the expression of this subject (the possessors). The most natural, and also an admissible explanation, is, that yshbw refers to the houses, and that למו, which can be used not only of persons, but also of things, is <hi type="italic">dat. ethicus. </hi> The meaning, however, is not: which are uninhabited, which would not be expressed as future, but rather by אין בהם יושׁב or similarly, but: which shall not inhabit, i.e., shall not be inhabited to them (ישׁב to dwell = to have inhabitants, as <reference osisRef="Isa.13.10">Isa 13:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.13">Jer 50:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.39">Jer 50:39</reference>, and freq.), or, as we should express it, which ought to remain uninhabited. <div eID="gen7504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7505" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Job.15.29">Job 15:29</reference> begins the conclusion: (because he has acted thus) he shall not be rich (with a personal subject as Hos 12:9, and יעשּׁר to be written with a sharpened שׁ, like יעצר above, <reference osisRef="Job.12.15">Job 12:15</reference>), and his substance shall not endure (קוּם, to take place, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.7">Isa 7:7</reference>; to endure, <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.14">1Sa 13:14</reference>; and hold fast, <reference osisRef="Job.41.18">Job 41:18</reference>), and מנלם shall not incline itself to the earth. The interpretation of the older expositors, <hi type="italic">non extendet se in terra,</hi> is impossible - that must be בּארץ eb tsum taht - elbi ינּטה; whereas <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> is commonly used in the intransitive sense to bow down, bend one’s self or incline (Ges. §53, 2). But what is the meaning of the subject מנלם? We may put out of consideration those interpretations that condemn themselves: לם מן, <hi type="italic">ex iis</hi> (Targ.), or לם מן, <hi type="italic">quod iis,</hi> what belongs to them (Saad.), or מלּם, their word (Syr. and Gecatilia), and such substitutions as σκιάν (צלם or צללם) of the lxx, and <hi type="italic">radicem</hi> of Jerome (which seems only to be a guess). Certainly that which throws most light on the signification of the word is כּנּלתך (for כּהנלתך with <hi type="italic">Dag. dirimens,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Job.17.2">Job 17:2</reference>), which occurs in Isa 33:1. The oldest Jewish lexicographers take this הנלה (parall. התם .ll) as a synonym of כּלּה in the signification, to bring to an end; on the other hand, Ges., Knobel, and others, consider כּכלּתך to be the original reading, because the meaning <hi type="italic">perficere</hi> is not furnished for נלה from the Arab. <hi type="italic">nâl</hi>, and because נל, standing thus together, is in Arabic an incompatible root combination (Olsh. §9, 4). This union of consonants certainly does not occur in any Semitic root, but the Arab. <hi type="italic">nâla</hi> (the long <hi type="italic">a</hi> of which can in the inflection become a short changeable bowel) furnishes sufficient protection for this one exception; and the meaning <hi type="italic">consequi,</hi> which belongs to the Arab. <hi type="italic">nâla ,</hi> fut. <hi type="italic">janı̂lu ,</hi> is perfectly suited to <reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">Isa 33:1</reference> : if thou hast fully attained (<hi type="italic">Hiph.</hi> as intensive of the transitive <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>, like הזעיק, הקנה) to plundering. If, however, the verb נלה is established, there is no need for any conjecture in the passage before us, especially since the improvement nearest at hand, מכלם (Hupf. מגּלה), produces a sentence (<hi type="italic">non figet in terra caulam</hi>) which could not be flatter and tamer; whereas the thought that is gained by Olshausen’s more sensible conjecture, מגּלם (their sickle does not sink to the earth, is not pressed down by the richness of the produce of the field), goes to the other extreme.<note placement="foot">Carey proposes to take מנלם = נמלם, their cutting, layer for planting; but the verb-group מלל, מול, נמל (vid., supra, p. 224) is not favourable to the supposition of a substantive נמל in this signification, according to the usual application of the language.</note> <div eID="gen7505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7506" type="x-p"/> Juda b. Karisch (Kureisch) has explained the word correctly by Arab. <hi type="italic">mnâlhm :</hi> that which they have offered (from <hi type="italic">nâla , janûlu</hi>) or attained (<hi type="italic">nâla , janı̂lu</hi>), i.e., their possession<note placement="foot">Freytag has erroneously placed the infinitives nail and manâl under Arab. <hi type="italic">nâl med. Wau</hi>, instead of under Arab. <hi type="italic">nâl me. Je</hi>, where he only repeats <hi type="italic">nail</hi>, and erroneously gives <hi type="italic">manâl</hi> the signification <hi type="italic">donum</hi>, citing in support of it a passage from <hi type="italic">Fâkihat al-chulafâ</hi>, where <hi type="italic">'azîz al-manâl</hi> (a figure borrowed from places difficult of access, and rendered strong and impregnable by nature or art) signifies “one who was hard to get at” (i.e., whose position of power is made secure). The true connection is this: Arab. <hi type="italic">nâl med</hi>. <hi type="italic">Wau</hi> signifies originally to <hi type="italic">extend</hi>, <hi type="italic">reach</hi>, to hand anything to any one with outstretched arm or hand, the correlatum Arab. <hi type="italic">nâl med. Je:</hi> to attain, i.e., first to touch or reach anything with outstretched arm or hand, and then really to grasp and take it, gen. <hi type="italic">adipisci, consequi, assequi, impetrare</hi>, with the ordinary infinitives <hi type="italic">nail</hi> and <hi type="italic">manâl</hi>. Therefore <hi type="italic">manâl</hi> (from Arab. <hi type="italic">nâl med. Je</hi>) signifies primarily as abstract, attainment; it may then, however, like <hi type="italic">nail</hi> and the infinitives generally, pass over to the concrete signification: what one attains to, or what one has attained, gotten, although I can give no special example in support of it. - Fl.</note> (not: their perfection, as it is chiefly explained by the Jewish expositors, according to נלה = כלה). When the poet says, “their prosperity inclines not to the ground,” he denies to it the likeness to a field of corn, which from the weight of the ears bows itself towards the ground, or to a tree, whose richly laden branches bend to the ground. We may be satisfied with this explanation (Hirz., Ew., Stickel, and most others): מנלם from מנלה (with which Kimchi compares מכרם, Num 20:19, which however is derived not from מכרה, but from מכר), similar in meaning to the post-biblical ממון, μαμωνᾶς; the suff., according to the same change of number as in <reference osisRef="Job.15.35">Job 15:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.20.23">Job 20:23</reference>, and freq., refers to רשׁעים. <div eID="gen7506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7507" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Job.15.30">Job 15:30</reference>, also, a figure taken from a plant is interwoven with what is said of the person of the ungodly: the flame withers up his tender branch without its bearing fruit, and he himself does not escape darkness, but rather perishes by the breath of His mouth, i.e., God’s mouth (<reference osisRef="Job.4.9">Job 4:9</reference>, not of his own, after <reference osisRef="Isa.33.11">Isa 33:11</reference>). The repetition of יסוּר (“he escapes not,” as <reference osisRef="Prov.13.14">Pro 13:14</reference>; “he must yield to,” as 1Ki 15:14, and freq.) is an impressive play upon words.
entries.162f4aa258ba9f28501c73fa3b3397a0ade41c4b: Job 15:31-35 31  Let him not trust in evil-he is deceived, <div eID="gen7507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7508" type="x-p"/> For evil shall be his possession. 32  His day is not yet, then it is accomplished, <div eID="gen7508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7509" type="x-p"/> And his palm-branch loseth its freshness. 33  He teareth off as a vine his young grapes, <div eID="gen7509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7510" type="x-p"/> And He casteth down as an olive-tree his flower. 34  The company of the hypocrite is rigid, <div eID="gen7510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7511" type="x-p"/> And fire consumeth the tents of bribery. 35  They conceive sorrow and bring forth iniquity, <div eID="gen7511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7512" type="x-p"/> And their inward part worketh self-deceit. אל does not merely introduce a declaration respecting the future (Luther: he will not continue, which moreover must have been expressed by the Niph.), but is admonitory: may he only not trust in vanity (<hi type="italic">Munach</hi> here instead of <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi>, according to the rule of transformation, <hi type="italic">Psalter</hi>, ii. 504, §4) - he falls, so far as he does it, into error, or brings himself into error (נתעה,   3 <hi type="italic">praet.,</hi> not <hi type="italic">part.,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Niph.</hi> like <reference osisRef="Isa.19.14">Isa 19:14</reference>, where it signifies to be thrust backwards and forwards, or to reel about helplessly), - a thought one might expect after the admonition (Olsh. conjectures נתעב, one who is detestable): this trusting in evil is self-delusion, for evil becomes his exchange (תּמוּרה not <hi type="italic">compensatio</hi>, but <hi type="italic">permutatio, acquisitio</hi>). We have translated שׁוא by “evil” (<hi type="italic">Unheil</hi>), by which we have sought elsewhere to render און, in order that we might preserve the same word in both members of the verse.
